## 5.8 Complex Powers, Roots of Unity & de Moivre's Theorem

Because Euler's formula writes any complex number in polar form as $z = r e^{i\theta}$, raising a complex number to the $n$-th power simply raises its radius to $r^n$ while multiplying its angle by $n\theta$ (**Abraham de Moivre's theorem**), and taking an $n$-th root divides its angle into $n$ equally spaced spokes around the circle:
$$z = r e^{i\theta} \implies z^n = r^n e^{i n \theta} = r^n (\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta))$$
$$\sqrt[n]{z} = r^{1/n} \left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}\right)\right], \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1$$

Even more generally, on the SC-32 the binary complex power operator `[↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` evaluates $\mathbf{z}_2^{\mathbf{z}_1} = e^{\mathbf{z}_1 \ln(\mathbf{z}_2)}$ when *both* the base and the exponent are complex numbers! To evaluate $(1 + i)^{(1 - i)}$, we load the base $\mathbf{z}_2 = 1 + i$ into $(T, Z)$ (`1 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]`), load the exponent $\mathbf{z}_1 = 1 - i$ into $(Y, X)$ (`1 [ENTER] 1 [+/-]`), and press `[↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` to obtain **$2.807879 + 1.317865i$**:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `1 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]` | $0.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $1.0000$ | Base $z_2 = 1 + i$ loaded into $(T, Z)$ |

## 5.9 Complex Parallel Impedance: Admittance Inversion vs. Direct `CMPLX x∥y`

Across AC circuit analysis, RF impedance matching, and electro-acoustics, the SC-32's transient `[↰] [CMPLX]` prefix gives you two complementary ways to evaluate parallel complex impedances in Registers $(Y, X)$.

When you want to inspect the physical **conductance $G$ and susceptance $B$** of each parallel branch ($\mathbf{Y}_k = 1/\mathbf{Z}_k = G_k + jB_k$), use **Reciprocal Admittance Summation (`[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]`)**. For $\mathbf{Z}_1 = 20 + 15i\,\Omega$ and $\mathbf{Z}_2 = 10 - 25i\,\Omega$, inverting each branch in place shows you the inductive admittance $\mathbf{Y}_1 = 0.0320 - 0.0240i\,\text{S}$ and capacitive admittance $\mathbf{Y}_2 = 0.0138 + 0.0345i\,\text{S}$ before you add (`[↰] [CMPLX] [+]`) and invert back (`[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]`) to get $\mathbf{Z}_{\text{parallel}} = \mathbf{20.7516 - 4.7507i\,\Omega}$. Similarly, in the conjugate Zobel loudspeaker network analyzed at the close of this chapter ($\mathbf{Z}_1 = 3 + 4i$, $\mathbf{Z}_2 = 3 - 4i$), admittance inversion exposes why the opposite susceptances $\mp 0.16i\,\text{S}$ cancel identically, leaving pure real conductance $2G = 0.24\,\text{S} \implies \mathbf{4.166667\,\Omega}$.

When you simply want the equivalent parallel impedance in the fewest keystrokes, use the **Single-Stroke Complex Parallel Operator (`[↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y]`)**: load $\mathbf{Z}_1$ into $(T, Z)$ and $\mathbf{Z}_2$ into $(Y, X)$ (`20 [ENTER] 15 [ENTER] 10 [ENTER] 25 [+/-]`) and press `[↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y]` to evaluate $\frac{\mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{Z}_2}{\mathbf{Z}_1 + \mathbf{Z}_2} = \mathbf{20.7516 - 4.7507i\,\Omega}$ in one operation, saving eight keystrokes.

The same dual-pathway verification certifies complex exponentials and logarithms: keying `0 [↱] [π] [↰] [CMPLX] [eˣ]` evaluates $e^{i\pi}$ via `[↰] [CMPLX] [eˣ]` to yield $-1.0000000000 + 0.0000000000i$, which can be inverted immediately via `[↰] [CMPLX] [LN]` to recover $0.0000000000 + 3.1415926536i$.

## 5.10 Numerical Boundary Conditions & Singularity Guards

> **Complex Prefix Annunciator Arming**  
> Press [↰] [CMPLX]. The LCD annunciator bar displays `[↰] [CMPLX]`. If pressed by mistake, press `[C]` to cancel without displacing or clearing stack values.

> **Complex Division Operand Alignment**  
> When calculating $\mathbf{z}_{\text{num}} / \mathbf{z}_{\text{den}}$:
> * The **numerator** $\mathbf{z}_{\text{num}}$ must be loaded into Registers $(T, Z)$ first.
> * The **denominator** $\mathbf{z}_{\text{den}}$ must be loaded into Registers $(Y, X)$ second.
> * If the resulting quotient is inverted, press `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` to take the complex reciprocal in place.

> **Singularity Handling (Division by Zero Complex)**  
> Attempting complex division by $0 + 0i$ (`0 [ENTER] 0`) immediately halts execution and triggers `Error 02: DIVIDE BY 0`. The stack remains unmodified.

> **Hyperbolic and Inverse Trig Boundary Guards**  
> Under SC-32 firmware specifications, complex domain operations are supported for algebraic powers, roots, exponentials, logs, and direct trigonometric functions (`SIN`, `COS`, `TAN`). Attempting [↰] [CMPLX] `[↰] [ASIN]` or [↰] [CMPLX] `[↰] [HYP]` raises `Error 01: INVALID DATA`, directing the user to logarithmic conformal mappings.

## 5.11 AC Power Grids, Impedance Matching, and RF Transmission Lines in the Complex Plane

In AC electrical engineering, determining the equivalent impedance of a parallel RLC branch $Z_{\text{eq}} = \frac{Z_1 Z_2}{Z_1 + Z_2}$ requires evaluating complex numbers in polar or rectangular form *([Horowitz & Hill, 2015](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-horowitz2015))*:

$$Z_{\text{eq}} = \frac{(50 + 25i) \times (10 - 40i)}{(50 + 25i) + (10 - 40i)}$$
On algebraic scientific calculators, complex arithmetic requires typing clumsy multi-character strings with explicit imaginary unit `i` keys and double parentheses for every complex operand. A single misplaced parenthesis scrambles real resistance with imaginary reactance, producing erroneous phase angles that can destroy prototype RF amplifier stages *([Parker, 2019](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-parker2019))*.

On the SC-32, the $(Y, X)$ stack allocation represents the two-dimensional complex plane natively ($Y = \text{Real},\; X = \text{Imaginary}$) *([HP, 1982](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982))*. With the dedicated complex evaluator `[↰] [CMPLX]`, complex multiplication, division, reciprocals, and square roots execute in place. In addition, the parallel operator `[x∥y]` solves parallel complex impedances in a single keystroke, eliminating 18 algebraic button presses and completely preventing real/imaginary crosstalk.

---

### 5.11.1 Complex Arithmetic Primitives & De Moivre Roots in `CMPLX` Mode

We begin by exercising the paired $(Y, X)$ complex plane architecture on conjugate products, principal square roots, microwave scattering parameters, and quarter-wave transmission line transformers.

#### Complex Conjugate Multiplication & Modulus Squared

In the complex plane, a number $z = x + iy = r e^{i\theta}$ and its **complex conjugate** $z^* = x - iy = r e^{-i\theta}$ are mirror reflections across the real axis. When you multiply them together, their opposite phase angles cancel ($\theta + (-\theta) = 0^\circ$), collapsing the product onto the positive real axis at the squared Euclidean length $|z|^2 = x^2 + y^2$. For $z = 6 + 8i$, let us verify that $z \cdot z^*$ lands on the real axis with zero imaginary residual:

$$z^* = 6 - 8i \implies z \cdot z^* = 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100 + 0i$$

Keying `6 [ENTER] 8 [ENTER]` loads $z = 6 + 8i$ into the upper register pair $(T, Z)$, and entering the conjugate pair `6 [ENTER] 8 [+/-]` into $(Y, X)$ followed by `[↰] [CMPLX] [×]` in `6 [ENTER] 8 [ENTER] 6 [ENTER] 8 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [×] [x⇄y]` multiplies $(T + Zi)(Y + Xi)$ and drops the stack by two levels, leaving $(Y = 100.0000,\; X = \mathbf{100})$—confirming **$\text{Real} = 100.0$, $\text{Imag} = 0.0$**.

#### Complex Square Root of Pure Imaginary Unit: $\sqrt{i}$

When 16th-century algebraists first encountered $i = \sqrt{-1}$, critics feared that taking the square root of $i$ itself ($\sqrt{i}$) would require inventing yet another "more imaginary" dimension outside the complex plane. Carl Friedrich Gauss and Jean-Robert Argand proved that the complex plane is algebraically closed: on the *Unit Circle Volvelle*, $i = 0 + 1i$ is simply a unit vector pointing straight up at $90^\circ$ ($\pi/2\text{ rad}$), so taking its principal square root takes the square root of its unit length ($\sqrt{1} = 1$) while bisecting its angle in half to **$45^\circ$** ($\pi/4\text{ rad}$) in the first quadrant—the exact $45^\circ$ phase angle of Warburg electrochemical diffusion and RF skin-effect impedance:

$$\sqrt{i} = \sqrt{0 + 1i} = e^{i\pi/4} = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}i \approx 0.707107 + 0.707107i$$

Entering the pure imaginary unit $0 + 1i$ with `0 [ENTER] 1` (placing Real $= 0$ in $Y$ and Imag $= 1$ in $X$) and executing `0 [ENTER] 1 [↰] [CMPLX] [√x]` evaluates the complex square root in place, leaving $Y = \mathbf{0.707107}$ and $X = \mathbf{0.7071067812}$.

#### Two-Port S-Parameter Reflection Coefficient Transformation

When an RF engineer characterizes a microwave filter or cellular antenna on a Vector Network Analyzer (VNA), the instrument measures the input **scattering parameter** $S_{11}$—the complex ratio of the reflected voltage wave to the incident voltage wave. Suppose a port exhibits $S_{11} = 0.25 - 0.40i$. What is its **Return Loss ($\text{RL}$)** in decibels (how many dB the reflected wave is suppressed below the incident carrier)?

$$|S_{11}| = \sqrt{0.25^2 + (-0.40)^2} = \sqrt{0.0625 + 0.1600} = \sqrt{0.2225} \approx 0.471699$$
$$\text{RL} = -20 \log_{10}(0.471699) = 6.527\text{ dB}$$

Loading $S_{11}$ via `0.25 [ENTER] 0.40 [+/-]` and bridging to polar coordinates with `[x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r]` leaves phase $\theta = -1.012197\text{ rad}$ ($-58.0^\circ$) in Register $Y$ and reflection magnitude $|S_{11}| = 0.471699$ in Register $X$. Completing the sequence `0.25 [ENTER] 0.40 [+/-] [↰] [▸θ,r] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×] [+/-]` converts that magnitude directly into Return Loss $\text{RL} =$ **`6.5266998468`** $\text{dB}$ (and if you also need the standing wave ratio $\text{VSWR} = (1+|S_{11}|)/(1-|S_{11}|) = 2.786$, pressing `[↰] [LASTX]` right after `[↰] [LOG]` recovers $|S_{11}|$).

#### Quarter-Wave Transmission Line Impedance Inverter

How do you match a $Z_L = 100\,\Omega$ patch antenna to a $Z_0 = 50\,\Omega$ transmitter feedline without lumped inductors or capacitors? A transmission line segment of length $\ell = \lambda/4$ ($90^\circ$ of electrical phase shift one way, or $180^\circ$ round-trip across the Smith Chart) acts as a hardware **impedance inverter** $Z_{\text{in}} = Z_{\text{line}}^2 / Z_L$. Choosing the quarter-wave section's characteristic impedance as the geometric mean $Z_{\text{line}} = \sqrt{Z_0 Z_L} = \sqrt{50 \times 100} \approx 70.7107\,\Omega$ transforms the $100\,\Omega$ load into an exact $50\,\Omega$ input match:

$$Z_{\text{in}} = \frac{70.7107^2}{100.0} = \frac{5000.0}{100.0} = 50.00\,\Omega$$

Squaring $Z_{\text{line}} = 70.7107\,\Omega$ in place and dividing by $Z_L = 100\,\Omega$ via `70.7107 [↰] [x²] 100 [÷]` confirms the **$50.0000\,\Omega$** impedance match:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `70.7107` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $70.7107$ | Enter line characteristic impedance $Z_0$ |
| 2 | `[↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $5000.0031$ | Square characteristic impedance $Z_0^2$ |
| 3 | `100 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$50.0000$** | Divide by load resistance $Z_L$; matched $Z_{\text{in}} = 50.0\,\Omega$ |

### 5.11.2 Complex Roots, Analytic Continuation & Audio Crossover Filters

The next seven models explore de Moivre's principal roots, complex circular functions (where sines and cosines can grow larger than $1$), and the transfer functions of Butterworth and Linkwitz-Riley loudspeaker crossovers.

#### Complex Cube Roots of $-8$: $\sqrt[3]{-8}$

On the real number line, the equation $z^3 = -8$ has the familiar negative root $z = -2$. In the complex plane, however, $-8$ sits on the negative real axis at polar angle $\theta = \pi\text{ rad}$ ($180^\circ$): $z^3 = 8 e^{i\pi}$. By de Moivre's theorem, its three cube roots sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle on a circle of radius $8^{1/3} = 2$, starting with the **principal root** at one-third of the angle ($\theta_0 = \pi/3 = 60^\circ$):

$$z_0 = 8^{1/3} e^{i\pi/3} = 2 \left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2(0.5 + 0.866025i) = 1.0 + 1.732051i$$

Loading the base $z_2 = -8 + 0i$ into $(T, Z)$ (`8 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER]`) and evaluating the cube root via `8 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 0.333333333333 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ] [x⇄y]` yields **`1`** in Register $X$, or forming the exact rational exponent $z_1 = 1/3 + 0i$ in $(Y, X)$ via `8 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 0.333333333333 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]` evaluates the principal branch $e^{(1/3)\ln(-8)} = 2 e^{i\pi/3}$ to full precision, yielding $(Y = \mathbf{1.000000},\; X = \mathbf{1.7320508075})$.

#### Complex Sine Evaluation: $\sin(1 + 2i)$

For a real angle $x$, $\sin x$ is trapped forever between $-1$ and $+1$. What happens when we feed a complex argument $z = x + iy = 1 + 2i$ into `[↰] [CMPLX] [SIN]`? By Euler's definition $\sin z = (e^{iz} - e^{-iz})/(2i)$, the imaginary component $iy$ becomes a real exponential $e^{\mp y}$, coupling circular oscillation along $x$ with hyperbolic growth ($\cosh y, \sinh y$) along $y$—which is why $\sin(1 + 2i)$ has a magnitude greater than $3.7$!

$$\sin(x + iy) = \sin x \cosh y + i \cos x \sinh y$$
$$\text{Real} = \sin(1)\cosh(2) \approx 0.841471 \times 3.762196 = 3.165779, \quad \text{Imag} = \cos(1)\sinh(2) \approx 0.540302 \times 3.626860 = 1.959601$$

Keying `1 [ENTER] 2` to load $1 + 2i$ into $(Y, X)$ and executing `1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [SIN]` evaluates the complex sine in place, producing $(Y = \mathbf{3.165779},\; X = \mathbf{1.9596010414})$.

#### Complex Cosine Evaluation: $\cos(1 + 2i)$

By the same Euler expansion, the complex cosine $\cos(x + iy)$ describes damped standing waves on lossy transmission lines and evanescent waveguide modes:

$$\cos(x + iy) = \cos x \cosh y - i \sin x \sinh y$$
$$\text{Real} = \cos(1)\cosh(2) = 0.540302 \times 3.762196 = 2.032723, \quad \text{Imag} = -\sin(1)\sinh(2) = -0.841471 \times 3.626860 = -3.051898$$

Entering $1 + 2i$ and evaluating the complex cosine via `1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [COS]` yields $(Y = \mathbf{2.032723},\; X = \mathbf{-3.051897799})$.

#### Fundamental Identity Verification: $\sin^2(z) + \cos^2(z) = 1$

Even though $\sin(1+2i)$ and $\cos(1+2i)$ in our complex sine and cosine evaluations above grew far outside $[-1, +1]$, the principle of **analytic continuation** guarantees that the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 z + \cos^2 z = 1$ still holds across the entire complex plane! Let us square both complex outputs and add them together on the stack:

$$\sin^2(1+2i) + \cos^2(1+2i) = (6.182115 + 12.407147i) + (-5.182115 - 12.407147i) = 1.000000 + 0.000000i$$

Notice how the large $\pm 12.407147i$ imaginary cross-terms cancel each other while $6.182115 - 5.182115$ collapses back to $1.000000$ (and if you chain the calculation directly from $z = 1+2i$ via `1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [SIN] [↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²] 1 [ENTER] 2 [↰] [CMPLX] [COS] [↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²] [↰] [CMPLX] [+]`, it holds to full 64-bit precision):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `3.165779 [ENTER] 1.959601` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $3.165779$ | $1.959601$ | Load $\sin(1+2i)$ from above |
| 2 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $6.182115$ | $12.407147$ | Square complex sine $(\sin z)^2$ |
| 3 | `2.032723 [ENTER] 3.051898 [+/-]` | $6.182115$ | $12.407147$ | $2.032723$ | $-3.051898$ | Load $\cos(1+2i)$ from above |
| 4 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` | $6.182115$ | $12.407147$ | $-5.182115$ | $-12.407147$ | Square complex cosine $(\cos z)^2$ |
| 5 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $6.182115$ | $6.182115$ | **$1.000000$** | **$0.000000$** | Sum squares: $\sin^2 z + \cos^2 z = 1 + 0i$ |

#### Butterworth 2nd-Order Low-Pass Filter Transfer Function

In 1930, British engineer Stephen Butterworth designed the "maximally flat" low-pass filter $H(s) = 1 / (s^2 + \sqrt{2}s + 1)$ so that passband ripple vanishes completely. At the normalized cutoff frequency $s = j\omega/\omega_c = 0 + 1i$ (e.g., $f_c = 2,500\text{ Hz}$), the $s^2 = -1$ term and the $+1$ constant in the denominator $B_2(j) = s^2 + \sqrt{2}s + 1$ cancel identically, leaving only the damping term $0 + j\sqrt{2}$:

$$s^2 = -1 + 0i, \quad \sqrt{2} s = 0 + 1.414214i \implies B_2(j) = (-1 + 1) + 1.414214i = 0 + 1.414214i$$
$$H(j) = \frac{1}{0 + 1.414214i} = 0 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}i = 0 - 0.707107i \implies |H| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx -3.01\text{ dB}$$

Loading $B_2(j) = 0 + 1.414214i$ into $(Y, X)$ and inverting in place via `0 [ENTER] 1.414214 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` (or exact `0 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]`) directly evaluates the complex transfer function $H(j) = \mathbf{0.000000 - 0.707107i}$—showing both the $-3.01\text{ dB}$ half-power attenuation ($|H| = 1/\sqrt{2}$) and the $-90^\circ$ phase lag at crossover.

#### Linkwitz-Riley 4th-Order Filter (Cascaded Butterworth)

Why do studio monitor loudspeakers rarely use a single 2nd-order Butterworth crossover? Because at the crossover frequency $s = j$, the low-pass output lags by $-90^\circ$ ($-i/\sqrt{2}$) while the high-pass output leads by $+90^\circ$ ($+i/\sqrt{2}$)—a $180^\circ$ phase opposition that causes a deep acoustic cancellation null! In 1976, Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley solved this by cascading *two* 2nd-order Butterworth filters in series (`LR4`), squaring the transfer function so both drivers sit at $-6.02\text{ dB}$ ($|H| = 0.5$) and are in phase at $-180^\circ$, summing acoustically back to unity gain ($0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0$, $0\text{ dB}$):

$$H_{\text{LR4}}(j) = [H_{\text{Butter2}}(j)]^2 = \left(-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = -0.500000 + 0.000000i \implies 20 \log_{10}(0.5) = -6.02\text{ dB}$$

Constructing $-i/\sqrt{2}$ in $(Y, X)$ with full precision and squaring in place via `0 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [1/x] [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` lands on exact Real **`-0.500000`** and Imag **`0.000000`**, from which `[x⇄y] [ABS] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×]` confirms the $-6.0206\text{ dB}$ crossover attenuation:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `0 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [1/x] [+/-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.707107$ | Construct exact Butterworth response $0 - i/\sqrt{2}$ |
| 2 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$-0.500000$** | **$0.000000$** | Evaluate $[H_{\text{Butter2}}]^2$; Real in $Y$, Imag in $X$ |
| 3 | `[x⇄y] [ABS]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.500000$ | Inspect Real component magnitude $\lvert H\rvert = 0.5$ |
| 4 | `[↰] [LOG] 20 [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$-6.020600$** | Calculate $-6.02\text{ dB}$ acoustic crossover attenuation |

#### Operational Amplifier Inverting Bandpass Gain

An inverting active bandpass filter uses a parallel RC feedback network $Z_f = 10\text{ k}\Omega \parallel 10\text{ nF}$ and a series RC input network $Z_{\text{in}} = 1\text{ k}\Omega + 100\text{ nF}$. At the center angular frequency $\omega = 10,000\text{ rad/s}$ ($f = 1,591.55\text{ Hz}$), where $1/(\omega C_f) = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ and $1/(\omega C_{\text{in}}) = 1\text{ k}\Omega$, the feedback and input impedances are $Z_f = 5000 - 5000i\,\Omega$ and $Z_{\text{in}} = 1000 - 1000i\,\Omega$. Find the complex voltage gain $A_v = -Z_f / Z_{\text{in}}$:

$$Z_f = \frac{10000}{1 + j} = 5000 - 5000i\,\Omega, \quad Z_{\text{in}} = 1000 - 1000i\,\Omega \implies A_v = -\frac{Z_f}{Z_{\text{in}}} = -\frac{5000(1 - i)}{1000(1 - i)} = -5.0 + 0i$$

Because both networks share the exact same $-45^\circ$ phase angle at $\omega_0 = 10,000\text{ rad/s}$, executing `5000 [ENTER] 5000 [+/-] [ENTER] 1000 [ENTER] 1000 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] [↰] [CMPLX] [+/-] [x⇄y]` cancels their reactive phase shifts completely via complex division and negation, yielding pure inverting gain $A_v = \mathbf{-5.000000}$ + **`-5`** $i$ ($13.98\text{ dB}$):

### 5.11.3 Bridge Circuits, Three-Phase Power & Conformal Mapping

The next five scenarios extend complex stack arithmetic to AC impedance bridges, three-phase power grids, mechanical suspension eigenvalues, ionized plasma sheaths, and Joukowsky airfoil aerodynamics.

#### Thevenin Equivalent Impedance of Bridge Circuit

To find the Thévenin output impedance looking into the detector terminals of an AC impedance bridge with upper/lower arms $Z_A = 10 + 20i\,\Omega$, $Z_C = 20 + 0i\,\Omega$ on the left and $Z_B = 30 - 10i\,\Omega$, $Z_D = 0 - 25i\,\Omega$ on the right, we short the excitation source and evaluate the series sum of two parallel complex branches:

$$Z_{\text{th}} = (Z_A \parallel Z_C) + (Z_B \parallel Z_D) = \left(\frac{140 + 80i}{13}\right) + \left(\frac{150 - 250i}{17}\right) \approx 19.5928 - 8.5520i\,\Omega$$

Look at how the SC-32's native complex parallel key `[↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y]` simplifies this bridge: instead of computing $(Z_A Z_C)/(Z_A + Z_C)$ by hand, `[↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y]` resolves each parallel arm in a single stroke:

| 3 | `30 [ENTER] 10 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 25 [+/-]` | $30.0000$ | $-10.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-25.0000$ | Load branch impedances $Z_B$ and $Z_D$ |
| 4 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y]` | $30.0000$ | $30.0000$ | $8.8235$ | $-14.7059$ | Parallel branch $Z_{BD} = Z_B \parallel Z_D$ |
| 5 | `10.7692 [ENTER] 6.1538 [↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $8.8235$ | $8.8235$ | **$19.5928$** | **$-8.5520$** | Sum branches: $Z_{\text{th}} = Z_{BD} + Z_{AC}$ |

#### Polyphase 3-Phase Symmetrical Components ($a$-Operator)

Why can a high-voltage three-phase transmission tower carry megawatts of power across three phase wires without needing a fourth neutral return cable? In 1918, Charles LeGeyt Fortescue introduced **symmetrical components** using the $120^\circ$ complex phase rotator $a = e^{i 120^\circ} = \cos(120^\circ) + i\sin(120^\circ) = -0.5 + 0.866025i$ and $a^2 = e^{i 240^\circ} = -0.5 - 0.866025i$. Because the three unit phasors $1$, $a$, and $a^2$ point $120^\circ$ apart like the three spokes of a Mercedes star, their vector sum vanishes identically ($1 + a + a^2 = 0$), meaning balanced three-phase currents cancel at the neutral point:

$$a = -0.5 + 0.866025i, \quad a^2 = -0.5 - 0.866025i \implies 1 + a + a^2 = \mathbf{0.000000 + 0.000000i}$$

In Degrees mode (`[DEG]`), we project the two unit phasors $1\angle 120^\circ$ and $1\angle 240^\circ$ into Gaussian complex coordinates via `[↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]`, sum them via `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]`, and add the reference phase $1 + 0i$ to verify exact zero-sequence cancellation:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `120 [ENTER] 1 [↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.500000$ | $0.866025$ | Polar to Gaussian: $a = -0.5 + 0.8660i$ |
| 2 | `240 [ENTER] 1 [↱] [▸y,x] [x⇄y]` | $-0.500000$ | $0.866025$ | $-0.500000$ | $-0.866025$ | Polar to Gaussian: $a^2 = -0.5 - 0.8660i$ |
| 3 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $-0.500000$ | $-0.500000$ | $-1.000000$ | $0.000000$ | Complex sum: $a + a^2 = -1.0 + 0.0i$ |
| 4 | `1 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $-1.000000$ | $-1.000000$ | **$0.000000$** | **$0.000000$** | Add $+1$ reference: $1 + a + a^2 = 0 + 0i$ |

#### Damped Harmonic Oscillator Complex Eigenvalues

Consider an underdamped mechanical suspension with sprung mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$, shock-absorber viscous damping $c = 8\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}$, and spring stiffness $k = 50\text{ N/m}$. Substituting $x(t) = e^{\lambda t}$ into $m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = 0$ yields the complex conjugate eigenvalues $\lambda = -\alpha \pm j\omega_d$:

$$\lambda = -\frac{c}{2m} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{c}{2m}\right)^2 - \frac{k}{m}} = -2.0 \pm \sqrt{4 - 25} = -2.0 \pm \sqrt{-21} = -2.0 \pm 4.582576i$$

Computing the real damping rate $\alpha = -c/(2m) = -2.0\text{ s}^{-1}$ in Register $Y$ and the damped ringing frequency $\omega_d = \sqrt{21} \approx \mathbf{4.582576\text{ rad/s}}$ in Register $X$ places the complete complex eigenvalue pair $\lambda = -2.0 \pm 4.5826i$ right on the stack:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `8 [ENTER] 4 [÷] [+/-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-2.0000$ | Real damping factor $\alpha = -c/(2m) = -2.0\text{ s}^{-1}$ |
| 2 | `4 [ENTER] 25 [-] [+/-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-2.0000$ | $21.0000$ | Discriminant magnitude $\lvert\Delta\rvert = 21.0$ |
| 3 | `[√x]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-2.0000$ | **$4.582576$** | Damped angular frequency $\omega_d = 4.5826\text{ rad/s}$ |
| 4 | `[↱] [SHOW]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$-2.000000$** | **$4.582576$** | Complex conjugate eigenvalues $\lambda = -2.0 \pm 4.5826i$ |

> **Automotive Shock Absorbers & Skyscraper Tuned Mass Dampers:**  
> Look at the physical meaning of the two registers in Step 4: Register $Y$ ($\alpha = -2.0\text{ s}^{-1}$) is the **viscous shock-absorber decay rate** set by oil forced through piston orifices ($c = 8\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}$), which dissipates road-impact energy into heat so the chassis settles in $\tau = 1/|\alpha| = 0.50\text{ s}$; Register $X$ ($\omega_d = 4.5826\text{ rad/s}$) is the **reactive ringing frequency** at which kinetic energy in the $2\text{ kg}$ sprung mass and potential energy in the $50\text{ N/m}$ coil spring exchange back and forth $90^\circ$ out of phase. If the shock absorber seals leak ($c \to 0$), the eigenvalue slides horizontally onto the pure imaginary axis ($\lambda = \pm j\omega_n = \pm 5.0i\text{ rad/s}$) and the car bounces indefinitely; if damping is increased to $c_{\text{crit}} = 2\sqrt{mk} = 20\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}$ ($\zeta = 1$), the imaginary part in Register $X$ vanishes ($\omega_d = 0$) for deadbeat critical damping.

#### Plasma Physics Dielectric Permittivity

When a spacecraft re-enters the atmosphere wrapped in an ionized plasma sheath (or when shortwave radio bounces off the ionosphere), free electrons oscillate at the plasma frequency $\omega_p$ while colliding with neutral gas atoms at collision frequency $\nu$. In the Appleton-Hartree Drude model, these collisions make the plasma's relative permittivity $\epsilon_r$ complex:

$$\epsilon_r = 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega - j\nu)}$$

For $\omega_p = 10^7\text{ rad/s}$, wave frequency $\omega = 2 \times 10^7\text{ rad/s}$, and collision rate $\nu = 5 \times 10^6\text{ s}^{-1}$, normalizing all frequencies by $\omega_p = 10^7\text{ rad/s}$ gives $\omega_p = 1, \omega = 2, \nu = 0.5$, so the normalized denominator is $\omega(\omega - j\nu) = 2(2 - 0.5i) = 4.0 - 1.0i$. Inverting $4 - i$ in place via `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]`, negating with `[↰] [CMPLX] [+/-]`, and adding $1 + 0i$ yields $\epsilon_r = \mathbf{0.764706 - 0.058824i}$ (where the real part $< 1$ bends radio waves via refraction and the imaginary part measures collisional attenuation):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `4 [ENTER] 1 [+/-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $4.0000$ | $-1.0000$ | Scaled denominator $z = 4.0 - 1.0i$ |
| 2 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] [↰] [CMPLX] [+/-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.235294$ | $-0.058824$ | Negated reciprocal $-1/(4-i)$ |
| 3 | `1 [ENTER] 0` | $-0.235294$ | $-0.058824$ | $1.0000$ | $0.0000$ | Unit real reference $1.0 + 0i$ in $(Y, X)$ |
| 4 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $-0.235294$ | $-0.235294$ | **$0.764706$** | **$-0.058824$** | Add unity: $\epsilon_r = 0.7647 - 0.0588i$ |

#### Conformal Mapping: Joukowsky Airfoil Transformation

How did early aerodynamicists calculate the lift of a curved airplane wing before wind tunnels and supercomputers? In 1910, Russian aviation pioneer Nikolai Zhukovsky (Joukowsky) discovered that the analytic complex mapping $\zeta = z + c^2/z$ **conformally maps** the simple, exact streamline flow around a slightly offset circular cylinder in the $z$-plane into the cambered, rounded-leading-edge, sharp-trailing-edge profile of an aircraft wing in the $\zeta$-plane! Because every differentiable complex function satisfies Laplace's equation ($\nabla^2\phi = 0$), transforming the circle automatically transforms the airflow streamlines around the wing. For a cylinder boundary point $z = 1.1 + 0.2i$ with scale $c = 1.0$, find the corresponding airfoil coordinate $\zeta$:

$$\frac{1}{z} = \frac{1.1 - 0.2i}{1.21 + 0.04} = \frac{1.1 - 0.2i}{1.25} = 0.88 - 0.16i \implies \zeta = z + \frac{1}{z} = (1.1 + 0.2i) + (0.88 - 0.16i) = \mathbf{1.980000 + 0.040000i}$$

By loading $z = 1.1 + 0.2i$ into both $(T, Z)$ and $(Y, X)$ (`1.1 [ENTER] 0.2 [ENTER] 1.1 [ENTER] 0.2`), inverting $(Y, X)$ in place with `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` ($\to 0.880000 - 0.160000i$), and adding the two together with `[↰] [CMPLX] [+]`, the Joukowsky transform maps the cylinder point to the airfoil surface at $(Y = \mathbf{1.980000},\; X = \mathbf{0.040000})$.

### 5.11.4 RF Transmission Lines, Eigenvalue Audits & Zobel Networks

Our closing trio applies complex square roots, complex squaring, and conjugate admittance cancellation to lossy telegrapher's transmission lines, quadratic complex roots, and constant-resistance Zobel loudspeaker networks.

#### Lossy Transmission Line Complex Characteristic Impedance ($Z_0$)

In an ideal lossless coaxial cable ($R' = G' = 0$), the characteristic impedance $Z_0 = \sqrt{L'/C'}$ is a pure real resistance ($50\,\Omega$). In a real physical cable with series copper resistance $R' = 0.1\,\Omega/\text{m}$, inductance $L' = 0.25\,\mu\text{H/m}$, dielectric shunt conductance $G' = 1\,\mu\text{S/m}$, and capacitance $C' = 100\,\text{pF/m}$ operating at $\omega = 10^7\text{ rad/s}$, Oliver Heaviside's telegrapher's equations yield a **complex characteristic impedance**:

$$Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R' + j\omega L'}{G' + j\omega C'}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.1 + 2.5i}{10^{-6} + 10^{-3}i}} \approx \mathbf{50.0095 - 0.9748i\,\Omega}$$

Loading the series impedance per meter $Z' = 0.1 + 2.5i$ into $(T, Z)$, the shunt admittance per meter $Y' = 10^{-6} + 10^{-3}i$ into $(Y, X)$, dividing via `[↰] [CMPLX] [÷]`, and taking the complex square root via `[↰] [CMPLX] [√x]` reveals how copper loss perturbs $Z_0$ to $\mathbf{50.0095 - 0.9748i\,\Omega}$:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `0.1 [ENTER] 2.5 [ENTER]` | $0.0000$ | $0.1000$ | $2.5000$ | $2.5000$ | Load series impedance $Z' = 0.1 + 2.5i$ |
| 2 | `1 [E] 6 [+/-] [ENTER] 1 [E] 3 [+/-]` | $0.1000$ | $2.5000$ | $1.0000 \times 10^{-6}$ | $1.0000 \times 10^{-3}$ | Load shunt admittance $Y'$ into $(Y, X)$ |
| 3 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [÷]` | $0.1000$ | $0.1000$ | $2499.9975$ | $-97.4999$ | Complex impedance ratio $Z'/Y'$ |
| 4 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [√x]` | $0.1000$ | $0.1000$ | **$50.0095$** | **$-0.9748$** | Characteristic impedance $Z_0 = \sqrt{Z'/Y'}$ |

#### Complex Root Finding of Quadratic with Real Coefficients

The characteristic polynomial $z^2 - 4z + 13 = 0$ has negative discriminant $\Delta = 16 - 52 = -36$, yielding the complex conjugate roots $z = (4 \pm \sqrt{-36})/2 = 2 \pm 3i$. Let us substitute $z_1 = 2 + 3i$ directly back into $z^2 - 4z + 13$ on the stack to watch the real and imaginary parts cancel simultaneously to zero:

$$(2+3i)^2 - 4(2+3i) + 13 = (-5 + 12i) - (8 + 12i) + 13 = \mathbf{0.0 + 0.0i}$$

Squaring $z_1 = 2 + 3i$ in place (`2 [ENTER] 3 [↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` $\to -5 + 12i$), subtracting $4z_1 = 8 + 12i$ (`8 [ENTER] 12 [↰] [CMPLX] [-]` $\to -13 + 0i$), and adding $13 + 0i$ (`13 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [+]`) verifies zero residual across both registers:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `2 [ENTER] 3` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $2.0000$ | $3.0000$ | Candidate complex root $z_1 = 2 + 3i$ loaded |
| 2 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [↰] [x²]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-5.0000$ | $12.0000$ | Complex square $z_1^2 = -5 + 12i$ in place |
| 3 | `8 [ENTER] 12 [↰] [CMPLX] [-]` | $-5.0000$ | $-5.0000$ | $-13.0000$ | $0.0000$ | Subtract $4z_1 = 8 + 12i$ |
| 4 | `13 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [+]` | $-13.0000$ | $-13.0000$ | **$0.0000$** | **$0.0000$** | Add $13 + 0i$; residual $= 0.0 + 0.0i$ |

#### Chained Complex Admittance Evaluation

Audio engineers wire a **Zobel impedance-compensation network** ($R - jX_C$) in parallel with an inductive loudspeaker voice coil ($R + jX_L$) so that the amplifier sees a purely resistive load. Let us compute the parallel combination of conjugate branches $Z_1 = 3 + 4i\,\Omega$ and $Z_2 = 3 - 4i\,\Omega$:

$$\frac{1}{Z_{\text{parallel}}} = \frac{1}{3+4i} + \frac{1}{3-4i} = \frac{3-4i}{25} + \frac{3+4i}{25} = \frac{6}{25} \implies Z_{\text{parallel}} = \frac{25}{6} = \mathbf{4.166667\,\Omega}$$

Because the opposite susceptances $\mp 4/25 = \mp 0.16i\,\text{S}$ cancel identically when the two conjugate admittances are added, we only need to invert $Z_1 = 3 + 4i$ (`3 [ENTER] 4 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` $\to Y = 0.120000,\; X = -0.160000$), swap the real conductance $G = 0.12\,\text{S}$ into Register $X$ (`[x⇄y]`), double it (`2 [×]`), and invert (`[1/x]`) via `3 [ENTER] 4 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] [x⇄y] 2 [×] [1/x]` to obtain $Z_{\text{parallel}} = \mathbf{4.166667\,\Omega}$ (or in one stroke via `3 [ENTER] 4 [ENTER] 3 [ENTER] 4 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y]`):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `3 [ENTER] 4` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $3.0000$ | $4.0000$ | Load branch impedance $Z_1 = 3 + 4i$ |
| 2 | `[↰] [CMPLX] [1/x]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.120000$ | $-0.160000$ | Invert: $Y_1 = 0.12 - 0.16i\,\text{S}$ |
| 3 | `[x⇄y]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.160000$ | $0.120000$ | Swap real conductance to Register $X$ |
| 4 | `2 [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.160000$ | $0.240000$ | Double conductance (imag parts cancel) |
| 5 | `[1/x]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $-0.160000$ | **$4.166667$** | Invert net conductance: $Z_{\text{parallel}} = 4.1667\,\Omega$ |

# Chapter 6: Analytic & Solid Geometry, Surface Area & Mensuration

## 6.1 The Heat Sink, the Rocket Nozzle & Surface-to-Volume Scaling

In his 1638 treatise *Two New Sciences* (*Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze*) *([Galilei, 1638](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-galilei1638))*, **Galileo Galilei** formulated the geometric **Square-Cube Law**: scaling any physical body by a linear factor $\ell$ multiplies its heat-dissipating and load-bearing surface area by the square ($\ell^2$) while multiplying its heat-generating volume and mass by the cube ($\ell^3$). Across biology, thermodynamics, aerodynamic friction, chemical catalysis, and semiconductor cooling, that $A/V \propto \ell^2 / \ell^3 = 1/\ell$ scaling asymmetry is the governing physical bottleneck.

Inside a modern high-performance microprocessor, billions of nanometer-scale transistors switch at gigahertz frequencies, generating localized thermal flux exceeding $100\text{ W/cm}^2$ *([Incropera et al., 2007](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-incropera2007))*—a power density approaching the heat flux inside a nuclear reactor core. Under Fourier's Law of Thermal Conduction and Newton's Law of Cooling *([Incropera et al., 2007](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-incropera2007))*, convective heat removal from a solid boundary to an ambient fluid is governed by:

$$\dot{Q} = h \cdot A_{\text{surface}} \cdot (T_{\text{solid}} - T_{\text{fluid}})$$

Because the heat dissipation rate $\dot{Q}$ is directly proportional to exposed surface area $A_{\text{surface}}$, inadequate boundary area causes internal junction temperatures to soar. This physical law links microprocessor pin-fin heat sinks directly to biological thermoregulation across the animal kingdom:
* **Why Hummingbirds Enter Torpor While Elephants Grow Ear-Fins:** A $3\text{-gram}$ **ruby-throated hummingbird** ($\ell \approx 2\text{ cm}$) has a massive surface-area-to-volume ratio ($A/V \propto 1/\ell$), radiating body heat so rapidly relative to its tiny thermal mass that its heart must beat $1,200\text{ times per minute}$ by day and plunge into deep hypothermic **torpor** at night to avoid starving. Conversely, a $5,000\text{-kilogram}$ **African elephant** ($\ell \approx 200\text{ cm}$—a $100\times$ linear scale-up that multiplies heat-producing volume by $100^3 = 1,000,000\times$ while multiplying skin area by only $100^2 = 10,000\times$) has $1/100\text{th}$ the relative cooling surface and would fatally overheat without pumping blood through huge, thin, vascularized **ear-fins**.
* **Extruded Silicon Heat Sinks:** A high-power microprocessor faces the exact elephant bottleneck: machining or extruding aluminum into dozens of parallel fins adds no volume—in fact, it removes material—yet it multiplies the effective convective surface area by more than $2,500\%$.

In real-world aerospace enclosures and consumer instruments, geometry is never composed of tidy textbook cubes. Enclosures feature drafted mold tooling angles, filleted stress-relief radii, cylindrical fastener bosses, and compound chamfers. Rather than scribbling fragile intermediate area calculations across scratch paper, the engineer audits the physical artifact polygon by polygon directly on the RPN stack:
* Primary exterior faces accumulate into the statistical bus via `[Σ+]`.
* Internal mounting apertures, screw countersinks, and display cutouts subtract via `[↰] [Σ-]`.
* The LCD counter ($n = 1, 2, 3 \dots$) tracks every verified face.
* Recalling `[↱] [SUMS]` → `Σx` instantly produces the certified boundary surface area.

Rather than transcribing individual face measurements onto paper and keying a fragile chain of parenthesized products, the StackCalc SC-32 maps each physical face directly onto the **Statistical Accumulator Bus (`[Σ+]`)**.

### 6.3.1 2D Plane Area Primitives & The Contest Mensuration Canon
The SC-32 evaluates 2D plane geometric regions using rapid, parenthesis-free RPN keystroke pipelines. In high-speed STEM tournaments and engineering analysis, these primitives collapse multi-step trigonometric and radical reductions into continuous tactile reductions:

| **Circular Segment** | $A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 (\theta - \sin\theta)$ | Sector area minus triangular chord core ($\frac{1}{2} r^2 \sin\theta$). | `θ [ENTER] [SIN] [-] r [↰] [x²] [×] 2 [÷]` |

| **Parabolic Segment** | $A = \frac{2}{3} b h$ | Archimedes' quadrature: segment is exactly $\frac{4}{3}$ of inscribed triangle. | `b [ENTER] h [×] 2 [×] 3 [÷]` |
| **Regular $n$-gon** | $A = \frac{1}{4} n s^2 \cot(\pi/n)$ | Decomposition into $n$ congruent central isosceles triangles. | `[↱] [π] n [÷] [TAN] [1/x] s [↰] [x²] [×] n [×] 4 [÷]` |
| **Cyclic Quadrilateral** | $A = \sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}$ | Brahmagupta's formula: 4-term cyclic extension of Heron's formula. | Four stack factors multiplied inside-out $\to$ `[√x]` |

For the master quick-reference tables of all 2D plane sections and perimeter formulas, consult **[Appendix D: Section 7 (Coordinate Geometry, Mensuration & 2D Curved Sections)](sc32/appendix-d-constants-and-equations.md)**.

Instead of computing $R^2$ and $r^2$ separately and subtracting, keying `R [ENTER] r [-] R [ENTER] r [+] [×] [↱] [π] [×]` avoids large squaring operations and preserves precision when $R \approx r$ (thin-walled pressure vessel shells and flanged pipe gaskets).

### 6.3.2 Ramanujan's Second Perimeter Approximation for Ellipses

One of the great surprises of classical geometry is that while the *area* of an ellipse with semi-axes $(a, b)$ is the effortless product $A = \pi a b$ (a circle of radius $b$ stretched along one axis by $a/b$), its *perimeter* has no closed-form expression in elementary functions! Measuring the arc length of an ellipse requires evaluating a complete elliptic integral of the second kind—which is where elliptic integrals got their name.

In 1914, Indian mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan published a remarkable algebraic approximation that achieves sub-parts-per-million accuracy across nearly all engineering eccentricities by defining the dimensionless flattening parameter $h = \frac{(a - b)^2}{(a + b)^2}$:
$$h = \frac{(a - b)^2}{(a + b)^2}, \qquad P \approx \pi (a + b) \left[ 1 + \frac{3h}{10 + \sqrt{4 - 3h}} \right]$$
On the SC-32 stack, Ramanujan's nested radical evaluates from the inside out without a single parenthesis: form $h = ((a - b)/(a + b))^2$, evaluate $\sqrt{4 - 3h}$ in Register $X$, add $10$ and invert via `[1/x]`, multiply by $3h$, add $1$, and scale by $\pi(a + b)$.

### 6.3.3 Heron's Formula for Arbitrary Triangles

When a surveyor or structural engineer measures the three side lengths $(a, b, c)$ of a triangular gusset plate or land parcel, finding a perpendicular altitude $h$ by trigonometry takes extra steps. In the 1st century CE, **Heron of Alexandria** showed in his *Metrica* that the area of any triangle follows directly from its **semiperimeter** $s = (a + b + c)/2$ alone:
$$s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}, \qquad A = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$$

Suppose a triangular parcel has sides $a = 7.0\text{ m}$, $b = 9.0\text{ m}$, and $c = 12.0\text{ m}$. Watch how storing $s$ in Variable `S` lets you build the four-factor product cleanly on the stack:
1. **Compute and store the semiperimeter $s$:** Key `7 [ENTER] 9 [+] 12 [+] 2 [÷]` (`7 [ENTER] 9 [+] 12 [+] 2 [÷]`) to obtain $s = 14.0\text{ m}$ in Register $X$, and store it via `[STO] S`.
2. **Accumulate the three $(s - \text{side})$ factors:** Since $s = 14.0$ is already sitting in Register $X$, simply key `7 [-]` to get $(s - a) = 7.0$; then key `[RCL] S 9 [-] [×]` to multiply by $(s - b) = 5.0$ ($\to 35.0$); then key `[RCL] S 12 [-] [×]` to multiply by $(s - c) = 2.0$ ($\to 70.0$).
3. **Multiply by $s$ and extract the root:** Key `[RCL] S [×] [√x]` to evaluate $\sqrt{14.0 \times 70.0} = \sqrt{980.0} = \mathbf{31.304952\text{ m}^2}$:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `7 [ENTER] 9 [+] 12 [+] 2 [÷] [STO] S` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $14.0000$ | Semiperimeter $s = (a+b+c)/2$ stored in `S` |
| 2 | `7 [-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $7.0000$ | Factor $(s - a) = 14 - 7 = 7.0$ directly from $X$ |
| 3 | `[RCL] S 9 [-] [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $35.0000$ | Multiply by $(s - b) = 5.0$; subtotal $= 35.0$ |
| 4 | `[RCL] S 12 [-] [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $70.0000$ | Multiply by $(s - c) = 2.0$; subtotal $= 70.0$ |
| 5 | `[RCL] S [×] [√x]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$31.304952$** | Multiply by $s$ and take root; Area $= 31.30\text{ m}^2$ |

## 6.4 The Master Surface Area Technique via Stats Mode (`[Σ+]`)

In mechanical CAD, thermal design, and additive manufacturing, finding the total exterior surface area of a 3D part is traditionally a bookkeeping headache. Real-world enclosures have top and bottom lids, side walls, end caps, bosses, and cutout apertures. On an algebraic calculator, summing all those faces requires a fragile string of parenthesized products:
$$A_{\text{total}} = (2 \times L \times W) + (2 \times L \times H) + (2 \times W \times H) + \dots$$
where a single mistyped digit at face #5 forces you to re-key the entire expression from the beginning.

### 6.4.1 Turning the Statistical Accumulator (`[Σ+]`) into a Polygon Tally Bus

On the StackCalc SC-32, the **Statistical Accumulator (`[Σ+]`)** serves as a dedicated hardware summing bus that decouples each face calculation from the running total:

First, press `[CLΣ]` to clear the six internal statistical registers ($\Sigma x = 0, n = 0$). Next, compute the area $A_1$ of your first face (or symmetric face pair) on the stack and press `[Σ+]`. That single keystroke adds $A_1$ into the internal $\Sigma x$ summation register, increments the polygon counter to $n = 1$, displays $1.0000$ in Register $X$ so you can verify how many face groups you have tallied, and arms the stack for your next face calculation! If you need to deduct a window cutout or screw bore—or if you accidentally push a wrong dimension—simply compute that area and press `[↰] [Σ-]` to subtract it from $\Sigma x$ without disturbing any previous faces. Once every boundary face has been tallied, pressing `[↱] [SUMS]` recalls the exact total surface area $\Sigma x$ at full 12-digit precision—with **zero parentheses, zero named memory variables, and zero scratch paper**.

### 6.4.2 Scratchpad Mensuration vs. Register-Preserving Geometric Accumulation

### 6.4.3 Galileo's Square-Cube Law, L-Frame Annuli & Polyhedral Face Decomposition

To see why surface-area-to-volume scaling and the `[Σ+]` statistical bus work together so naturally, combine three physical tools from the StackCalc studio kit:
1. **Counting Tiles & Galileo's Square-Cube Asymmetry:** Dock a single $19.0 \times 19.0 \times 7.0\text{ mm}$ ($1\text{U}$) counting tile on the Snapfinity lid: it has $1$ top unit face, $1$ bottom unit face, and $4$ perimeter side edges ($6$ outer block faces). Now dock eight $1\text{U}$ tiles into a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ block prism (four $2\text{-tile}$ towers docked in a $2 \times 2$ square): doubling the block count along each axis ($\ell \to 2\ell$) multiplies the exposed exterior surface area by $2^2 = 4$ ($6 \to 24\text{ exposed block faces}$), while multiplying the internal volume by $2^3 = 8$ ($1 \to 8\text{ tiles}$)—physically demonstrating Galileo's 1638 Square-Cube Law. Conversely, halving the edge length of a unit cube ($\ell \to \frac{1}{2}\ell$) packs **$2^3 = 8$ half-size cubes into each unit volume** while doubling the total exposed surface area ($A/V \to 2\times$), which is why finely divided catalyst pellets, pulmonary alveoli, and pin-fin heat sinks pack massive active surface area into a compact volume.
2. **The Algebra Factoring L-Frame Stage & Difference-of-Squares Annuli:** When evaluating a flanged pipe gasket or hollow structural tube $A = \pi(R^2 - r^2) = \pi(R - r)(R + r)$, docking an $R \times R$ square flat into the $90^\circ$ L-Frame Stage and removing an $r \times r$ corner square leaves an L-shaped gnomon whose two wings rearrange directly into a single $(R - r) \times (R + r)$ rectangle.
3. **Isohedral Polyhedra & Planar Face Accumulation (`[Σ+]`):** Inspecting the five Platonic polyhedra ($d4$ tetrahedron, $d6$ cube, $d8$ octahedron, $d12$ dodecahedron, and $d20$ icosahedron) among the **Polyhedral Dice** confirms Leonhard Euler's topological invariant ($V - E + F = 2$) and reveals why you never need a monolithic 30-character algebraic formula for surface area: every three-dimensional solid is simply a boundary collection of $F$ planar faces. Computing each planar face (or opposing face pair) on the 4-level stack and pressing `[Σ+]` accumulates the area into $\Sigma x$ while the LCD counter $n = 1, 2, \dots$ verifies that every face of the solid has been accounted for.

## 6.5 Solid Mensuration: Volumes of Classical 3D Geometries & The Contest Canon

The evaluation of three-dimensional solids in competitive contests and engineering stress analysis demands rapid, error-free reductions. The following master catalog pairs each classical geometry with its physical motivation and optimal RPN evaluation pipeline:

| 3D Solid Geometry | Analytical Volume Formula | Total External Surface Area Formula | Physical & Geometric Motivation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Rectangular Prism** | $V = l \cdot w \cdot h$ | $A = 2(lw + lh + wh)$ | Cartesian volume product; 6 orthogonal bounding faces. |
| **Right Circular Cylinder** | $V = \pi r^2 h$ | $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$ | Extrusion of circular base along normal axis $h$. |
| **Right Circular Cone** | $V = \frac{1}{3} \pi r^2 h$ | $A = \pi r^2 + \pi r \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$ | Exactly $\frac{1}{3}$ of circumscribed cylinder (Eudoxus-Archimedes). |
| **Sphere** | $V = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3$ | $A = 4\pi r^2$ | Surface area is derivative of volume with respect to radius $r$. |
| **Torus (Major $R$, minor $r$)** | $V = 2\pi^2 R r^2$ | $A = 4\pi^2 R r$ | **Pappus-Guldinus:** Centroid path ($2\pi R$) $\times$ disk area ($\pi r^2$) or perimeter ($2\pi r$). |
| **Frustum of Right Cone** | $V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h (R^2 + Rr + r^2)$ | $A = \pi(R^2 + r^2) + \pi(R + r)s$ | Truncated cone; factored in RPN via $(R+r)^2 - Rr$. |
| **Spherical Cap (height $h$)** | $V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h^2 (3r - h)$ | $A_{\text{dome}} = 2\pi r h$ | Archimedes' cylinder balance: sliced sphere disk integration. |
| **Spherical Zone (2 bases)** | $V = \frac{\pi h}{6}(3r_1^2 + 3r_2^2 + h^2)$ | $A_{\text{zone}} = 2\pi R h$ | Slice between two parallel cutting planes through a sphere. |
| **Ellipsoid** | $V = \frac{4}{3} \pi a b c$ | $A \approx 4\pi \left(\frac{(ab)^p + (ac)^p + (bc)^p}{3}\right)^{1/p}$ | Affine 3D stretch of sphere along 3 principal orthogonal axes. |
| **Paraboloid of Revolution** | $V = \frac{1}{2} \pi r^2 h$ | $A = \frac{\pi r}{6h^2} \left[(r^2 + 4h^2)^{3/2} - r^3\right]$ | Exactly $\frac{1}{2}$ of bounding cylinder (Archimedes' law of paraboloids). |
| **Cylindrical Ungula (Hoof)** | $V = \frac{2}{3} r^3 \tan\alpha$ | $A_{\text{curved}} = 2 r^2 \tan\alpha$ | Slicing cylinder by an inclined plane passing through base diameter. |
| **Universal Prismoidal Solid** | $V = \frac{h}{6}(A_{\text{top}} + 4A_{\text{mid}} + A_{\text{bot}})$ | Dependent on geometry | Simpson's 3D rule: exact for any solid whose area is a cubic polynomial in $z$. |
| **Regular Tetrahedron** | $V = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12} a^3$ | $A = \sqrt{3} a^2$ | 4 equilateral triangular faces; self-dual Platonic solid. |
| **Regular Octahedron** | $V = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} a^3$ | $A = 2\sqrt{3} a^2$ | 8 equilateral triangular faces; dual of the cube. |
| **Regular Dodecahedron** | $V = \frac{15 + 7\sqrt{5}}{4} a^3$ | $A = 3\sqrt{25 + 10\sqrt{5}}\,a^2$ | 12 regular pentagonal faces; golden ratio $\phi$ geometry. |
| **Regular Icosahedron** | $V = \frac{5(3 + \sqrt{5})}{12} a^3$ | $A = 5\sqrt{3} a^2$ | 20 equilateral triangular faces; dual of the dodecahedron. |

For the master quick-reference tables of all 3D solid mensuration formulas, consult **[Appendix D: Section 8 (3D Solid Mensuration & Revolution Geometry)](sc32/appendix-d-constants-and-equations.md)**.

To evaluate $V = \frac{\pi h}{3}(R^2 + Rr + r^2)$, avoid computing three separate squares and products. Factor the parenthetical term as $(R+r)^2 - Rr$:
> `R [ENTER] r [ENTER] [+] [↰] [x²] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] [×] [-] h [×] [↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]`

## 6.6 Analytic 3D Spatial Geometry: Distance, Centroid & Mass Moments of Inertia

Beyond static volumes and surface areas, three-dimensional structural and mechanical design requires spatial distance metrics, composite mass centroids, and rotational moments of inertia.

### 6.6.1 3D Spatial Euclidean Metric

In three-dimensional Cartesian space $\mathbb{R}^3$, the straight-line distance between two coordinate stations $P_1(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $P_2(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ follows the 3D Pythagorean theorem:
$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$$
On the SC-32, you evaluate this parenthesis-free by computing each coordinate difference, squaring it in place, and adding it to the running sum on the stack before extracting the square root:
`x2 [ENTER] x1 [-] [↰] [x²]  y2 [ENTER] y1 [-] [↰] [x²] [+]  z2 [ENTER] z1 [-] [↰] [x²] [+] [√x]`.

### 6.6.2 Center of Mass (Centroid) via Weighted Mean ($\bar{x}_w$)

When an aircraft or structural beam is assembled from $N$ discrete components, each with mass (or cross-sectional area) $m_k$ centered at coordinate $x_k$, the composite center of mass is the **mass-weighted average** of the coordinates:
$$\bar{x}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^N m_k x_k}{\sum_{k=1}^N m_k}$$
Because the SC-32's statistical engine accumulates both $\Sigma y$ and the cross-product sum $\Sigma xy$ whenever you press `[Σ+]`, you never need to calculate the numerator and denominator separately! Simply clear statistics (`[CLΣ]`), load each part's weight or mass $m_k$ into Register $Y$ and its coordinate $x_k$ into Register $X$, and press `[Σ+]`. Once all parts are entered, pressing `[x̄w]` (via the `[↱] [x̄,ȳ]` menu) immediately divides $\Sigma(m_k x_k)$ by $\Sigma m_k$ to return the exact centroid coordinate $\bar{x}_{\text{cm}}$.

### 6.6.3 Mass Moments of Inertia & Steiner's Parallel Axis Theorem

In rotational dynamics, mass alone does not determine how hard it is to spin a flywheel or robot arm; what matters is how far that mass sits from the axis of rotation, weighted by the *square* of the radial distance ($I = \int r^2\,dm$). For symmetric bodies of mass $M$ and outer radius $R$, the center-of-mass moment of inertia takes the form $I_{\text{cm}} = k M R^2$, where the dimensionless geometric factor $k$ measures how concentrated the mass is toward the outer rim: a **solid cylinder** spinning about its symmetry axis has $I_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$; a **solid sphere** (where mass crowds closer to the axis near the poles) has $I_{\text{cm}} = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$; a **thin spherical shell** has $I_{\text{cm}} = \frac{2}{3}MR^2$; and a **slender rod** of length $L$ spinning about its midpoint has $I_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$.

What if the body pivots about an offset axle displaced by a perpendicular distance $d$ from its center of mass—like a robotic arm link pivoting about its shoulder joint? **Jakob Steiner's Parallel Axis Theorem** proves that you never need to re-integrate over the solid; you simply add the point-mass transfer term $M d^2$ to the centroidal inertia:
$$I = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2$$
For a slender rod pivoted at one end ($d = L/2$), Steiner's theorem immediately gives $I_{\text{end}} = \frac{1}{12}ML^2 + M(L/2)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{4}\right)ML^2 = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$—four times the rotational inertia of spinning the same rod about its center!

## 6.7 3D Printer Slicing, Perimeter Shells, Gyroid Infill & Filament Mass Takeoff

Why does every Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) 3D slicer—when preparing the SC-32 enclosure or your $42.0\text{ mm}$ Gridfinity manipulative kits—have to calculate **both** the total exterior surface area $\Sigma A$ (via `[Σ+]` in the SC-32 handheld chassis surface area takeoff) and the enclosed interior volume $V$?

Unlike an injection-molded or cast metal part that is $100\%$ solid throughout, a 3D-printed engineering structure is a **composite sandwich shell** (just like the avian wing bones in Chapter 1):
1. **Solid Outer Perimeter Shells ($V_{\text{shell}} \approx A_{\text{surface}} \times N_{\text{walls}} \times w_{\text{line}}$):** The slicer first traces $N_{\text{walls}}$ solid perimeter loops (typically $3$ walls at $w_{\text{line}} = 0.45\text{ mm}$ width, for a $1.35\text{ mm}$ skin thickness $t_{\text{shell}}$) over the entire exterior boundary surface area $A_{\text{surface}} = \Sigma x$ accumulated by `[Σ+]`.
2. **Sparse Internal Gyroid Infill ($V_{\text{core}} = V_{\text{interior}} \times f_{\text{infill}}$):** The enclosed interior volume $V_{\text{interior}} = V_{\text{total}} - V_{\text{shell}}$ is filled not with solid plastic, but with a periodic minimal-surface **gyroid** or cubic lattice at $f_{\text{infill}} = 15\%\text{--}25\%$ relative density.
3. **Total Filament Mass & Spool Length Takeoff:** Multiplying the combined polymer volume by the density of PLA ($\rho \approx 1.24\text{--}1.25\text{ g/cm}^3 = 0.00124\text{ g/mm}^3$, or PETG at $1.27\text{ g/cm}^3$; compare the hexagonal fastener and brass bar mass takeoffs later in this chapter) predicts the exact part mass in grams:
   $$m_{\text{part}} = \rho \left( A_{\text{surface}} \cdot t_{\text{shell}} + V_{\text{interior}} \cdot f_{\text{infill}} \right)$$
   For the SC-32 chassis shell ($A_{\text{surface}} = 25,460\text{ mm}^2$ from our chassis surface area audit), over $70\%$ of the structural filament mass resides in the outer surface shell ($A_{\text{surface}} \cdot t_{\text{shell}}$)—explaining why `[Σ+]` surface area takeoffs are essential for additive manufacturing cost and weight estimation. And if any cutout or aperture needs to be deducted during the takeoff, a single tap of `[↰] [Σ-]` subtracts that face from $\Sigma x$ on the hardware statistical bus.

## 6.8 Numerical Boundary Conditions & Singularity Guards

> **Clearing Statistical Accumulators Before Mensuration**  
> Always execute `[CLΣ]` before beginning a multi-face surface area calculation. Verify that $n = 0$ and $\Sigma x = 0.0$ to ensure no leftover statistical survey or regression data corrupts your geometric summation.

> **Heron's Formula Degenerate Triangle Error**  
> If the sum of any two sides is less than or equal to the third side ($a + b \le c$), the triangle is geometrically impossible. In Heron's formula, $(s - c) \le 0$, resulting in a negative number under the radical. Attempting `[√x]` raises `Error 01: INVALID DATA`.

> **Frustum Diameter vs Radius Consistency**  
> When calculating the volume of conical or pyramidal frustums, verify whether your inputs are radii ($R, r$) or diameters ($D, d$). Using diameters in a radius formula produces a four-fold volume error.

## 6.9 Pressure Vessels, Orbital Shells, and Structural Cross-Sections on the Stack

Across mechanical, civil, and aerospace structures, difference-of-squares factoring, `[Σ+]` boundary-face accumulation, weighted-mean centroids (`[x̄w]`), and Steiner's parallel-axis theorem turn complex three-dimensional geometry into clean register arithmetic.

### 6.9.1 Planar Cross-Sections, Flanges & Classical Volumes

We begin with machine flange gaskets, octagonal sheet-metal blanks, conical storage hoppers, spherical liquid tanks, and tetrahedral trusses.

#### Circular Annulus Area (Flanged Pipe Gasket)

When bolting together an ASME B16.5 high-pressure flange joint, the required bolt preload depends on the seating contact area of the ring-shaped neoprene gasket—an **annulus** bounded by outer radius $R = 85.0\text{ mm}$ and inner pipe bore radius $r = 50.0\text{ mm}$. Rather than multiplying by $\pi$ twice ($\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$), we factor $\pi$ outside the difference of squares:

$$A = \pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi (85^2 - 50^2) = \pi (7225 - 2500) = 4725\pi \approx \mathbf{14,844.0253\text{ mm}^2}$$

Keying `85 [↰] [x²] 50 [↰] [x²] [-] [↱] [π] [×]` computes the squared outer radius $R^2 = 7,225$ (`85 [↰] [x²]`), subtracts the squared inner bore $r^2 = 2,500$ (`50 [↰] [x²] [-]`) to leave $4,725.0\text{ mm}^2$ in Register $X$, and scales by `[↱] [π] [×]` to return **`14,844.02529`** (**$14,844.03\text{ mm}^2$**, or $148.44\text{ cm}^2$).

#### Regular Octagon Enclosure Face Area

How do you find the area of a regular octagonal sheet-metal face plate of edge length $s = 65.0\text{ mm}$ without evaluating cotangents? Picture a regular octagon as a bounding square of width $(1 + \sqrt{2})s$ with four $45^\circ$ right-isosceles corner triangles of leg $s/\sqrt{2}$ clipped off the four corners. Subtracting those four corner triangles leaves $A = 2(1 + \sqrt{2})s^2 = 2\delta_S s^2$, where $\delta_S = 1 + \sqrt{2} \approx 2.414214$ is the **silver ratio**:

$$A = 2 (1 + \sqrt{2}) s^2 \approx 4.828427 \times 65^2 = 4.828427 \times 4225 = \mathbf{20,400.1047\text{ mm}^2}$$

Entering `2 [√x] 1 [+] 2 [×] 65 [↰] [x²] [×]` builds the octagonal shape multiplier $2(1 + \sqrt{2}) \approx 4.828427$ directly on the stack (`2 [√x] 1 [+] 2 [×]`), squares the edge length $s = 65\text{ mm}$ (`65 [↰] [x²]`), and multiplies (`[×]`) to yield **`20,400.1046`** (**$20,400.10\text{ mm}^2$**).

#### Conical Frustum Storage Hopper Volume

An agricultural grain hopper (or rocket nozzle section) is shaped as a **conical frustum**—a cone sliced flat by two parallel planes—with upper radius $R = 1.80\text{ m}$, lower discharge radius $r = 0.40\text{ m}$, and vertical height $h = 2.50\text{ m}$. Notice the geometric beauty of the frustum volume formula $V = \frac{h}{3}(\pi R^2 + \pi Rr + \pi r^2)$: it is the height $h$ multiplied by the average of three areas—the top circle $\pi R^2$, the bottom circle $\pi r^2$, and their **geometric mean** $\sqrt{(\pi R^2)(\pi r^2)} = \pi Rr$:

$$V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h (R^2 + R r + r^2) = \frac{2.5\pi}{3} (1.8^2 + 1.8(0.4) + 0.4^2) = \frac{2.5\pi}{3} (3.24 + 0.72 + 0.16) = \frac{2.5\pi}{3} (4.12) = \mathbf{10.7861\text{ m}^3}$$

Watch how `[↰] [LASTX]` in the sequence `1.8 [↰] [x²] 1.8 [ENTER] 0.4 [×] [+] 0.4 [↰] [x²] [+] [↱] [π] [×] 2.5 [×] 3 [÷]` lets you compute $R^2 + Rr + r^2$ while typing $1.8$ and $0.4$ only once: `1.8 [↰] [x²] [↰] [LASTX] 0.4 [×] [↰] [LASTX] [↰] [x²] [+] [+]` forms $4.12\text{ m}^2$ in Register $X$, and scaling by `[↱] [π] [×] 2.5 [×] 3 [÷]` produces **`10.786134777`** (**$10.7861\text{ m}^3$**, or $10,786.1\text{ liters}$).

#### Spherical Storage Tank Segment (Cap) Volume

In a petrochemical refinery, volatile liquefied gases are stored inside spherical **Hortonsphere** tanks of radius $R = 4.0\text{ m}$. When an ultrasonic level sensor measures liquid depth $h = 1.5\text{ m}$ at the bottom of the sphere, what volume of liquid sits in the tank? Slicing the sphere into horizontal disks of radius $\sqrt{R^2 - (R-z)^2}$ and integrating from $z = 0$ to $h$ yields Archimedes' **spherical cap** formula:

$$V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h^2 (3R - h) = \frac{\pi (1.5^2)}{3} (3(4.0) - 1.5) = \frac{2.25\pi}{3} (10.5) = 0.75\pi \times 10.5 = \mathbf{24.7400\text{ m}^3}$$

Running `4 [ENTER] 3 [×] 1.5 [-] 1.5 [↰] [x²] [×] [↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]` forms the factor $(3R - h) = 10.5\text{ m}$ via `4 [ENTER] 3 [×] 1.5 [-]`, recovers $h = 1.5\text{ m}$ from `LASTX` and squares it (`[↰] [LASTX] [↰] [x²] [×]`), and scales by `[↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]` to deliver **`24.740042147`** (**$24.7400\text{ m}^3$**, or $24,740.0\text{ liters}$).

#### Regular Tetrahedron Height, Area & Volume

Why does the volume of a regular tetrahedron of edge length $a = 50.0\text{ mm}$ have a factor of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}$? You can inscribe a regular tetrahedron inside a cube of edge $a/\sqrt{2}$ by drawing the face diagonals connecting four alternating corners of the cube. Slicing off the four right-angled corner pyramids—each of volume $\frac{1}{6}\text{cube}$—leaves the central tetrahedron occupying $1 - \frac{4}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$ of the cube's volume, or $V = \frac{1}{3}(a/\sqrt{2})^3 = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}a^3$:

$$h = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} a \approx \mathbf{40.8248\text{ mm}}, \qquad A = \sqrt{3} a^2 \approx \mathbf{4,330.1270\text{ mm}^2}, \qquad V = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12} a^3 = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12} (125,000) \approx \mathbf{14,731.3913\text{ mm}^3}$$

For the enclosed volume, keying `2 [√x] 12 [÷] 50 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [×]` evaluates $\sqrt{2}/12 \approx 0.117851$ (`2 [√x] 12 [÷]`), cubes the edge length $a = 50\text{ mm}$ (`50 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ]` $\to 125,000$), and multiplies (`[×]`) to return **`14,731.39127`** (**$14,731.39\text{ mm}^3$**).

#### Extruded Heat Sink Fin Array Surface Area via `[Σ+]`

Just as with the stepped machine casting above, notice that the $8$ fin tips ($1,600\text{ mm}^2$) plus the valley floor ($8,400\text{ mm}^2$) equal the original $10,000\text{ mm}^2$ top footprint—so extruding the $8$ fins adds their $16$ vertical side walls ($56,000\text{ mm}^2$), boosting total surface area from $20,000\text{ mm}^2$ to **$76,000.0\text{ mm}^2$** ($760.0\text{ cm}^2$, a $3.8\times$ thermal multiplier):

#### Direction Cosines of 3D Vector

A deep-space tracking radar locks onto an ascending launch vehicle at 3D displacement vector $\vec{V} = (850, 1100, 550)\text{ m}$, whose Euclidean range is $|\vec{V}| = \sqrt{850^2 + 1100^2 + 550^2} = 1,494.9916\text{ m}$. To orient the telemetry gimbal, we need its three **direction cosines**—the components of the unit vector $\hat{u} = \vec{V}/|\vec{V}|$ along the East ($x$), North ($y$), and Zenith ($z$) axes:

$$\cos\alpha = \frac{850}{1494.9916} = \mathbf{0.568565}\;(55.35^\circ), \quad \cos\beta = \frac{1100}{1494.9916} = \mathbf{0.735790}\;(42.63^\circ), \quad \cos\gamma = \frac{550}{1494.9916} = \mathbf{0.367895}\;(68.41^\circ)$$

Executing `1494.9916 [STO] [D] 850 [RCL] [D] [÷] 1100 [RCL] [D] [÷] 550 [RCL] [D] [÷]` stores the norm $D = 1494.9916\text{ m}$ in Variable `D` (or recovers it via `[↰] [LASTX]` after each division) and divides each coordinate, leaving all three direction cosines arrayed simultaneously across the stack as $(Z = 0.568565,\; Y = 0.735790,\; X = $ **`0.3678950437`** $)$, where $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1.000000$.

#### Mass Moment of Inertia of Flywheel with Rim & Web

Why do mechanical punch-press flywheels concentrate most of their cast-iron mass in a thick outer rim supported by a thin inner web? Because rotational kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ scales with the *square* of the radius! Consider an $85\text{ kg}$ flywheel consisting of a heavy outer annular rim ($M_{\text{rim}} = 65\text{ kg}$, inner radius $r_1 = 0.28\text{ m}$, outer radius $r_2 = 0.35\text{ m}$) and an inner solid disk web ($M_{\text{web}} = 20\text{ kg}$, radius $R = 0.28\text{ m}$):

$$I_{\text{rim}} = \frac{1}{2} M_{\text{rim}} (r_1^2 + r_2^2) = 0.5(65)(0.28^2 + 0.35^2) = \mathbf{6.52925\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}, \qquad I_{\text{web}} = \frac{1}{2} M_{\text{web}} R^2 = 0.5(20)(0.28^2) = \mathbf{0.78400\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}$$
$$I_{\text{total}} = I_{\text{rim}} + I_{\text{web}} = 6.52925 + 0.78400 = \mathbf{7.31325\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}$$

Evaluating `0.28 [↰] [x²] 0.35 [↰] [x²] [+] 65 [×] 2 [÷] [STO] A  0.28 [↰] [x²] 20 [×] 2 [÷] [RCL] A [+]` yields **`7.31325`** ($I_{\text{total}} = \mathbf{7.31325\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}$)—showing that even though the outer rim accounts for $76.5\%$ of the flywheel's mass, it contributes **$89.3\%$** of the total rotational inertia:

#### Steiner's Parallel Axis Theorem for Offset Robotic Link

A carbon-fiber robotic arm link of mass $m = 3.5\text{ kg}$ and length $L = 0.80\text{ m}$ has centroidal moment of inertia $I_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{12}mL^2 \approx 0.186667\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ about its midpoint. When the servo motor accelerates the link about a pivot joint at one end (displaced by $d = L/2 = 0.40\text{ m}$ from the center of mass), what is the effective rotational inertia $I_{\text{pivot}}$? By **Jakob Steiner's Parallel Axis Theorem**:

$$I_{\text{pivot}} = I_{\text{cm}} + m d^2 = 0.186667 + 3.5(0.40^2) = 0.186667 + 0.560000 = \mathbf{0.746667\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}$$

Keying `0.80 [↰] [x²] 3.5 [×] 12 [÷]  0.40 [↰] [x²] 3.5 [×] [+]` returns **`0.7466666667`**: shifting the pivot from the center of mass to the endpoint adds $md^2 = \frac{1}{4}mL^2 = 3 I_{\text{cm}}$, quadrupling the inertia to $I_{\text{pivot}} = \frac{1}{3}mL^2 = \mathbf{0.7467\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}$:

### 6.9.3 Spherical Excess, Triaxial Ellipsoids & Pressure Hulls

From flat and cylindrical machine elements, we now turn to non-Euclidean spherical geometry, Knud Thomsen's triaxial asteroid surface formula, hexagonal fastener mass takeoffs, conical spring wire lengths, and deep-ocean bathysphere hulls.

#### Spherical Triangle Area via Girard's Theorem

On a flat sheet of paper, the interior angles of every triangle sum to exactly $180^\circ$ ($\pi\text{ rad}$), regardless of how big or small the triangle is. On a curved sphere of radius $R$, however, great-circle geodesics bow outward so that the interior angles $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ of a spherical triangle *always* sum to more than $180^\circ$! In 1629, Dutch-French mathematician **Albert Girard** proved a stunning theorem (the ancestor of the Gauss-Bonnet theorem): the **spherical excess** $E_{\text{rad}} = (\alpha + \beta + \gamma - 180^\circ)\frac{\pi}{180^\circ}$ is directly proportional to the triangle's surface area $A = R^2 E_{\text{rad}}$.

Suppose a geodetic survey network on Earth ($R = 6,371.0\text{ km}$) forms a continental spherical triangle with interior angles $\alpha = 82.5^\circ$, $\beta = 68.2^\circ$, and $\gamma = 44.7^\circ$. Let us find the enclosed planetary surface area:

$$\text{Spherical Excess } E = (\alpha + \beta + \gamma - 180^\circ) = (82.5^\circ + 68.2^\circ + 44.7^\circ) - 180^\circ = 195.4^\circ - 180^\circ = 15.4^\circ$$
$$E_{\text{rad}} = 15.4^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} \approx 0.268781\text{ rad} \implies A = R^2 E_{\text{rad}} = 6371^2 \times 0.268781 \approx \mathbf{10,911,102.5\text{ km}^2}$$

Summing the three angles on the stack, subtracting $180^\circ$, converting the $15.4^\circ$ spherical excess into radians, and multiplying by $R^2 = 6,371^2\text{ km}^2$ yields **$10,911,102.50\text{ km}^2$** (roughly the area of Europe):

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes & State Analysis |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 1 | `82.5 [ENTER] 68.2 [+] 44.7 [+]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $195.4000$ | Interior angle sum $\alpha + \beta + \gamma$ in degrees |
| 2 | `180 [-]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $15.4000$ | Spherical excess $E = 15.4^\circ$ |
| 3 | `[↱] [π] [×] 180 [÷]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.268781$ | Excess in radians $E_{\text{rad}} \approx 0.268781\text{ rad}$ |
| 4 | `6371 [↰] [x²] [×]` | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | $0.0000$ | **$10911102.50$** | Spherical triangle area $A = R^2 E_{\text{rad}}$ in km² |

#### Ellipsoid Surface Area (Knud Thomsen Approximation)

While the *volume* of a triaxial ellipsoid with semi-axes $(a, b, c)$ is simply $\frac{4}{3}\pi abc$, its *surface area*—just like the perimeter of an ellipse—has no closed-form expression in elementary functions. In 2004, Danish mathematician Knud Thomsen discovered that taking a power mean of the three projected semi-axis products $(ab, ac, bc)$ with exponent $p = 1.6075$ approximates the exact Legendre elliptic integral to within $1.06\%$ across all aspect ratios! Let us estimate the surface area of a potato-shaped asteroid modeled as a triaxial ellipsoid with semi-axes $a = 15.0\text{ km}$, $b = 10.0\text{ km}$, and $c = 6.0\text{ km}$:

$$p \approx 1.6075 \implies A \approx 4\pi \left(\frac{(ab)^p + (ac)^p + (bc)^p}{3}\right)^{1/p}$$

With projected semi-axis products $ab = 150$, $ac = 90$, and $bc = 60$, notice how `[↰] [LASTX]` lets you raise all three products to the power $p = 1.6075$ without re-typing the exponent: keying `150 [ENTER] 1.6075 [yˣ] 90 [↰] [LASTX] [yˣ] 60 [↰] [LASTX] [yˣ] [+] [+] 3 [÷] 1.6075 [1/x] [yˣ] 4 [×] [↱] [π] [×]` averages $3148.23 + 1384.98 + 721.74 = 5254.95 / 3 = 1751.65$, extracts the $1/1.6075$ root ($\to 104.16$), and scales by $4\pi$ to yield an asteroid surface area of **$1,308.90\text{ km}^2$** ($1308.8986\text{ km}^2$).

#### Hexagonal Bolt Head Volume and Mass

Why do structural bolts and honeycombs use regular hexagons? A regular hexagon of side length $s = 10.0\text{ mm}$ partitions cleanly into six equilateral triangles of area $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2$, giving a total cross-sectional area of $A_{\text{hex}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2$. For a steel hex bolt head of side $s = 10.0\text{ mm}$, height $h = 12.0\text{ mm}$, and steel density $\rho = 7.85\text{ g/cm}^3$ ($0.00785\text{ g/mm}^3$), find the mass of the head in grams:

$$A_{\text{hex}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} s^2 = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} (100) \approx 259.8076\text{ mm}^2 \implies V = A_{\text{hex}} h = 3,117.69\text{ mm}^3 = 3.11769\text{ cm}^3$$
$$\text{Mass } m = 3.11769\text{ cm}^3 \times 7.85\text{ g/cm}^3 = \mathbf{24.4739\text{ grams}}$$

On the stack, form the hexagon constant $3\sqrt{3}/2 \approx 2.598076$ via `3 [√x] [↰] [LASTX] [×] 2 [÷]` (using `[↰] [LASTX]` to recover $3$ after taking its square root), multiply by $s^2 = 100\text{ mm}^2$ (`10 [↰] [x²] [×]`) and height $h = 12\text{ mm}$ (`12 [×]`), and convert $\text{mm}^3$ to grams via `1000 [÷] 7.85 [×]` to obtain **$24.4739\text{ grams}$**.

#### Conical Spiral (Helix) Arc Length

Before winding a tapered conical compression spring (with base radius $R_1 = 30\text{ mm}$, top radius $R_2 = 10\text{ mm}$, axial height $h = 60\text{ mm}$, and $N = 6\text{ active coils}$), a spring maker must cut the straight spring-steel wire blank of length $L$. Unwrapping the conical helix into three orthogonal displacement components—total circumferential travel $2\pi N R_m$ at the mean radius $R_m = (R_1 + R_2)/2 = 20\text{ mm}$, vertical axial rise $h = 60\text{ mm}$, and radial inward taper $R_1 - R_2 = 20\text{ mm}$—turns the arc-length integral into a 3D Pythagorean sum:

$$L \approx \sqrt{(2\pi N R_m)^2 + h^2 + (R_1 - R_2)^2} = \sqrt{(2\pi \times 6 \times 20)^2 + 60^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{753.98^2 + 3600 + 400} \approx \mathbf{756.63\text{ mm}}$$

Summing the three squared orthogonal displacements via `2 [↱] [π] [×] 6 [×] 20 [×] [↰] [x²] 60 [↰] [x²] [+] 30 [ENTER] 10 [-] [↰] [x²] [+] [√x]` returns **`756.6302`** (**$756.63\text{ mm}$**):

#### Moment of Inertia of Hollow Spherical Pressure Hull

A deep-ocean titanium bathysphere pressure hull has outer radius $R_2 = 1.10\text{ m}$, inner radius $R_1 = 0.98\text{ m}$, and titanium alloy density $\rho = 4,500\text{ kg/m}^3$. Its shell volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi(R_2^3 - R_1^3) \approx 1.63283\text{ m}^3$ gives a hull mass of $M = 7,347.74\text{ kg}$. To design its attitude-control thrusters, we need its rotational moment of inertia $I$ about any diameter—which is simply the inertia of a solid outer sphere minus a solid inner sphere:

$$I = \frac{2}{5} M \frac{R_2^5 - R_1^5}{R_2^3 - R_1^3} = \frac{2}{5}(7347.74) \frac{1.10^5 - 0.98^5}{1.10^3 - 0.98^3} = 2939.10 \times \frac{0.706589}{0.389808} \approx \mathbf{5,327.42\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}$$

Notice that if you substitute $M = \frac{4}{3}\pi\rho(R_2^3 - R_1^3)$ algebraically, the $(R_2^3 - R_1^3)$ factor cancels completely to leave $I = \frac{8}{15}\pi\rho(R_2^5 - R_1^5)$. When evaluating directly from the known hull mass $M = 7,347.74\text{ kg}$, the fifth-power difference $(R_2^5 - R_1^5) = 0.706589\text{ m}^5$ waits in Register $Y$ while $(R_2^3 - R_1^3) = 0.389808\text{ m}^3$ forms in Register $X$:

| 2 | `1.1 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] 0.98 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [-]` | $0.706589$ | $0.706589$ | $0.706589$ | $0.389808$ | Third-power difference $(R_2^3 - R_1^3)$ |

### 6.9.4 Classical Solids, Mass Moments of Inertia & Geometric Sprints

Our closing geometric explorations evaluate the Steinmetz bicylinder intersection, WGS84 planetary flattening, pyramidal roof takeoffs, right-triangle incircles, tubular drive shafts, and surface-to-volume ratios.

#### Volume of Intersection of Two Cylinders (Steinmetz Solid)

When two equal circular pipes of radius $r = 15.0\text{ mm}$ intersect at right angles (forming a groin vault in architecture or a cross-fitting in high-pressure piping), what is the volume and surface area of their common intersection—the **Steinmetz bicylinder**?

Archimedes (in *The Method*) and 3rd-century Chinese mathematician Liu Hui (who called it the *Mouhefanggai*, or "two square umbrellas") discovered something astonishing: if you slice the bicylinder horizontally at any height $z$, the cross-section is a **square** of side $2\sqrt{r^2 - z^2}$, whereas the cross-section of an inscribed sphere of radius $r$ at the same height is a **circle** of area $\pi(r^2 - z^2)$. Because the ratio of the square's area to the circle's area is $\frac{4}{\pi}$ at every single slice, Bonaventura Cavalieri's principle guarantees that the total volume of the bicylinder is $\frac{4}{\pi}$ times the sphere's volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$—causing $\pi$ to cancel out completely!

$$V = \frac{4}{\pi}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right) = \frac{16}{3} r^3 = \frac{16}{3} (15^3) = \mathbf{18,000.0\text{ mm}^3}, \qquad A = 16 r^2 = 16(15^2) = \mathbf{3,600.0\text{ mm}^2}$$

Evaluating `16 [ENTER] 3 [÷] 15 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [×]` yields the exact rational volume **$18,000.0\text{ mm}^3$**, and `15 [↰] [x²] 16 [×]` gives the surface area **$3,600.0\text{ mm}^2$**.

#### Oblate Spheroid Planetary Flattening

Because the Earth spins once every $23\text{ hr } 56\text{ min}$, centrifugal acceleration bulges the equator to $a = 6,378.137\text{ km}$ compared to the polar semi-minor axis $b = 6,356.752\text{ km}$—an equatorial bulge of $a - b = 21.385\text{ km}$. Geodesists specify this oblateness by the **reciprocal flattening** $1/f = a / (a - b)$:

$$\text{Flattening } f = \frac{a - b}{a} = 1 - \frac{b}{a} = \frac{6378.137 - 6356.752}{6378.137} = \frac{21.385}{6378.137} \approx \mathbf{\frac{1}{298.2572}}$$

Rather than typing the 7-digit equatorial radius `6378.137` twice, the sequence `6378.137 [ENTER] 6356.752 [-] 6378.137 [÷] [1/x]` duplicates $a$ into Register $Z$ on entry: keying `6378.137 [ENTER] [ENTER] 6356.752 [-]` forms $(a - b) = 21.385\text{ km}$ in Register $X$ while $a = 6,378.137\text{ km}$ drops into Register $Y$, and pressing `[x⇄y] [÷] [1/x]` resolves the reciprocal flattening **$298.2572$** (or rewrite $f = 1 - b/a$ via `6356.752 [ENTER] 6378.137 [÷] 1 [x⇄y] [-] [1/x]`).

Each of the four sloping roof planes is a trapezoid of area $A_{\text{face}} = \frac{1}{2}(12 + 4)\times 6.5 = 52.0\text{ m}^2$. #### Tangent Circles Incircle of Right Triangle

What is the radius $r$ of the largest cylindrical coolant pipe that can be tucked inside a right-angled triangular structural channel with legs $a = 15.0\text{ cm}$ and $b = 20.0\text{ cm}$? By the two-tangent theorem of Euclidean geometry, the tangent segments from the $90^\circ$ corner to the **incircle** form a little square of side $r$, while the remaining tangent segments along the legs—$(a - r)$ and $(b - r)$—fold onto the hypotenuse $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = 25.0\text{ cm}$ so that $c = (a - r) + (b - r)$. Solving for the inradius $r$ yields a wonderfully clean linear formula:

$$r = \frac{a + b - c}{2} = \frac{15 + 20 - 25}{2} = \frac{10}{2} = \mathbf{5.0000\text{ cm}} \qquad (\text{with circumradius } R = \frac{c}{2} = 12.5\text{ cm})$$

Running `15 [↰] [x²] 20 [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] 15 [ENTER] 20 [+] [x⇄y] [-] 2 [÷]` computes the hypotenuse $c = 25.0\text{ cm}$ in Step 1 (which can also be done via `15 [ENTER] 20 [↰] [▸θ,r]`), sums the legs $a + b = 35.0\text{ cm}$ in Step 2, subtracts $c$, and halves the result to yield the exact inradius **`5.0000`** (**$r = 5.0000\text{ cm}$**):

#### Polar Moment of Inertia of Thin Cylindrical Tube

Why are automotive and helicopter drive shafts hollow tubes rather than solid bars? Because under torsional twist, shear stress increases linearly from zero at the center to a maximum at the outer skin, so the **polar moment of inertia** $J = \int r^2\,dA = \frac{\pi}{2}(R_o^4 - R_i^4)$ scales with the **fourth power** of radius! Consider a hollow steel drive shaft with outer diameter $D_o = 80.0\text{ mm}$ ($R_o = 40\text{ mm}$) and inner bore diameter $D_i = 70.0\text{ mm}$ ($R_i = 35\text{ mm}$):

$$J = \frac{\pi}{2} (R_o^4 - R_i^4) = \frac{\pi}{2} (40^4 - 35^4) = \frac{\pi}{2} (2,560,000 - 1,500,625) = \frac{\pi}{2} (1,059,375) \approx \mathbf{1,664,071.76\text{ mm}^4}$$

Boring out the inner $70\text{ mm}$ core removes $(35/40)^2 = \mathbf{76.6\%}$ of the steel weight while retaining $1 - (35/40)^4 = \mathbf{41.4\%}$ of the solid shaft's torsional stiffness $J$ (and notice on the keypad that `40 [↰] [x²] [↰] [x²]` computes $40^4$ in three strokes):
