## 11.3 The Base-Preserving Percentage Invariant (`[↱] [%]`)

On standard commercial calculators, pressing the percentage key is fraught with peril: some models merely divide the active entry by 100, others multiply by the previous operand, and nearly all overwrite the base operand in the process. Worse still, keying `100 + 8% =` on many algebraic pocket calculators literally computes $100 + 0.08 = 100.08$!

On the StackCalc SC-32, the **Percentage Function (`[↱] [%]`)** is an invariant dyadic operator adhering strictly to William Kahan's non-destructive specification:

$$\text{Calculation: } \quad X \leftarrow \frac{Y \times X}{100}, \quad Y \leftarrow Y \text{ (Preserved)}, \quad \text{Lift} \leftarrow \text{TRUE}$$

| Register | State After Keying `[Base] [ENTER] [Rate] [↱] [%]` | Executive Function |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Register $Y$** | Base Amount (Preserved frozen in $Y$) | Base remains intact for subsequent total, discount, or alternative trial |
| **Register $X$** | Computed Percentage Amount: $(Y \times X) / 100$ | Tax, tip, commission, or margin dollar value |

Because the base amount remains frozen in Register $Y$ while the dollar percentage appears in Register $X$, you see *both* numbers on the screen before deciding what to do with them. If you are adding sales tax, markup, or a gratuity, press `[+]` to sum $Y + X$. If you are deducting a trade discount or withholding tax, press `[-]` to compute $Y - X$. And if you want to discard the base and keep only the percentage amount in $X$, a quick `[x⇄y] [R↓]` drops it off the stack.

Compare how this plays out on the invoice from the beginning of the chapter ($\$150.00$ at $8.25\%$ tax): on an algebraic calculator, typing `150 × 0.0825 =` displays $\$12.38$ and destroys the $\$150.00$ base, forcing you to re-type `+ 150 =` to reach $\$162.38$—and if the client asks to check a $10\%$ discount instead, you have to start over from scratch. On the SC-32, keying `150 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]` places $\$12.38$ in Register $X$ while holding $\$150.00$ in Register $Y$; pressing `[+]` yields $\$162.38$ in a single stroke, and keying `100 [ENTER] 8 [↱] [%]` on a $\$100.00$ baseline places the exact dollar amount ($\mathbf{8}$) in $X$ while freezing $100.00$ in $Y$.

## 11.4 Period-over-Period & Year-over-Year Performance (`[↱] [%CHG]`)

Corporate revenue growth, cost expansion, and quarterly margin velocity are measured by relative percentage change:

$$\%CHG = \frac{\text{New Value} - \text{Old Value}}{\text{Old Value}} \times 100$$

On the SC-32, the **Percent Change Function (`[↱] [%CHG]`)** is executed via Right Shift `[↱]` followed by `[%CHG]` using the natural chronological order **Old Value `[ENTER]` New Value `[↱] [%CHG]`**:

| Register | State Before `[↱] [%CHG]` | State After `[↱] [%CHG]` | Executive Role |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Register $Y$** | Old Value (Baseline) | Old Value (Preserved in $Y$) | Allows instant variance check: `[x⇄y] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] [-]` |
| **Register $X$** | New Value (Current) | $\frac{\text{New} - \text{Old}}{\text{Old}} \times 100$ | Relative rate of expansion/contraction (%) |
| **`LASTX`** | Previous operand | New Value | Retained for delta calculations |

Just like `[↱] [%]`, `[↱] [%CHG]` is non-destructive: the Old Value stays anchored in Register $Y$ and the New Value is saved in `LASTX`, so you can immediately recover the absolute dollar variance ($\text{New} - \text{Old}$) by pressing `[x⇄y] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] [-]`.

## 11.5 Cross-Metric Elasticity & Spread: The Multi-Metric Stack Advantage

The true computational superiority of the RPN operational stack emerges during **comparative multi-metric corporate analytics**. Suppose an executive is evaluating a software portfolio company whose **Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)** grew from $\$12.0\text{M}$ to $\$15.6\text{M}$ ($+30.00\%$), while **Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)** expanded from $\$2.4\text{M}$ to $\$2.88\text{M}$ ($+20.00\%$). Two questions immediately arise at the board table:
1. **The ARR vs. CAC Growth Spread ($\Delta \text{ARR}\% - \Delta \text{CAC}\%$):** By how many percentage points did revenue growth outpace acquisition cost growth?
2. **The Growth Elasticity Ratio ($\Delta \text{ARR}\% \div \Delta \text{CAC}\%$):** How many percentage points of top-line revenue growth did each percentage point of acquisition spending buy?

| Stack Register | Value Staged | Financial Meaning | Immediate Dyadic Operation |
| :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Register $T$** | $0.00$ | Top of stack | — |
| **Register $Z$** | $0.00$ | Holding register | — |
| **Register $Y$** | $+30.00\%$ | Metric A YoY Growth ($\Delta\text{ARR}\%$) | Base comparator |
| **Register $X$** | $+20.00\%$ | Metric B YoY Growth ($\Delta\text{CAC}\%$) | Active metric |

With both growth rates staged side-by-side in Registers $Y$ and $X$, pressing `[-]` immediately yields the **$+10.00\%$ Growth Spread**, and pressing `[÷]` yields the **$1.50\times$ Growth Elasticity Ratio**. On an algebraic calculator, answering the same question requires either jotting intermediate percentages on a notepad or typing a 30-character nested-parenthesis formula `(((15.6 - 12.0) / 12.0) * 100) - (((2.88 - 2.40) / 2.40) * 100)`.

## 11.6 The 5-Variable Time Value of Money (TVM) Architecture

The SC-32 features an onboard **Five-Variable Time Value of Money (TVM) Engine** accessed via Left Shift `[↰]` followed by `[TVM]` on the multi-action `[x∥y]` key (Row 7, Column 3).

| TVM Variable | LFU Softkey | Actuarial Description | Computational Units |
| :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **$N$** | `[N]` | Total number of compounding periods | Integer or fractional periods |
| **$I\%YR$** | `[I%YR]` | Periodic interest rate per compounding period | Percent per period (e.g. `6.5` for 6.5%/yr or `6.75/12` for monthly) |
| **$PV$** | `[PV]` | Present value (initial loan principal or investment) | Currency ($) |
| **$PMT$** | `[PMT]` | Periodic annuity payment amount | Currency ($ per period) |
| **$FV$** | `[FV]` | Future value (final balloon balance or accumulated savings) | Currency ($) |

### 11.6.1 The Master Actuarial TVM Equation & Hybrid Analytical-Bisection Engine
All five financial variables are bound together by a single conservation law—the universal compound interest annuity equation:

$$PV + PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right] (1 + i \cdot S) + FV (1 + i)^{-N} = 0$$

where $i = \frac{I\%YR}{100}$ is the periodic interest rate per compounding period stored in `[I%YR]`, $N$ is the total number of compounding periods stored in `[N]`, and $S = 0$ for End-of-Period payments (Ordinary Annuity, the default for loans and mortgages) or $S = 1$ for Beginning-of-Period payments (Annuity Due, the standard for equipment leases and tuition, flagged by the `BEGIN` annunciator and toggled via `[↰] [TVM] [BEG/END]`).

When you store any four of the five TVM variables and press the fifth softkey, the SC-32 solves for the unknown variable automatically. Four of the five variables have exact $\mathcal{O}(1)$ analytical closed-form solutions, with a smooth zero-interest limit ($a_{\overline{N}|i} = \frac{1 - (1+i)^{-N}}{i} \to N$ whenever $|i| < 10^{-14}$):
* **Solving for `FV`:** $FV = -\frac{PV + PMT \cdot (1 + i \cdot S) \cdot a_{\overline{N}|i}}{(1+i)^{-N}}$
* **Solving for `PV`:** $PV = -PMT \cdot (1 + i \cdot S) \cdot a_{\overline{N}|i} - FV(1+i)^{-N}$
* **Solving for `PMT`:** $PMT = -\frac{PV + FV(1+i)^{-N}}{(1 + i \cdot S) \cdot a_{\overline{N}|i}}$
* **Solving for `N`:** Inverted analytically via natural logarithms:
  $$N = -\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{\text{PMT}_{\text{adj}} - i \cdot FV}{\text{PMT}_{\text{adj}} + i \cdot PV}\right)}{\ln(1 + i)}, \qquad \text{PMT}_{\text{adj}} = PMT(1 + i \cdot S)$$
  (which simplifies cleanly to $N = -(PV + FV)/PMT$ when $|i| < 10^{-14}$).
* **Solving for `I%YR` (240-Interval Scan + 100-Iteration Bisection):** Because the polynomial $f(i) = PV + PMT(1 + i \cdot S)a_{\overline{N}|i}(i) + FV(1+i)^{-N} = 0$ has no closed-form algebraic inverse for $i$ when $N > 4$ (by the Abel-Ruffini theorem!), the SC-32 runs a two-stage numerical root finder: first, it sweeps **240 uniform subintervals** across $i \in [-0.9999, +10.0]$ ($-99.99\%$ to $+1000\%$ per period) to bracket the sign change $f(a) \cdot f(b) \le 0$; second, it refines that bracket across up to **100 bisection steps** until $|f(\text{mid})| < 10^{-12}$ or $(b - a)/2 < 10^{-13}$, returning $I\%YR = 100 \cdot i$ to full 64-bit precision.

### 11.6.2 Why Cash-Flow Sign Discipline Works Like Conservation of Energy
Notice that the right-hand side of the master TVM equation is **zero**. Think of your wallet—or a corporate treasury account—as a physical control volume in thermodynamics or a circuit node in Kirchhoff's Current Law:
- **Cash Inflows ($+$) are Positive:** Any cash flowing *into* your hands (the $\$350,000$ loan wire you receive at mortgage closing, the $\$27.50$ semi-annual coupon check from a bond, or the final maturity payout at the end of a CD) is entered as a **positive** number.
- **Cash Outflows ($-$) are Negative (`[+/-]`):** Any cash flowing *out* of your pocket (the $\$925.00$ purchase price you pay to buy a bond, the monthly $\$2,270.09$ mortgage check you mail to the bank, or a balloon payoff at the end of a commercial note) is entered as a **negative** number using `[+/-]`.

When every future payment and final balance is discounted back to the present moment ($t = 0$), the inflows and outflows must balance to zero. That immediately explains why entering all positive numbers ($PV = +1000, PMT = +50, FV = +1000$) triggers `ERROR 5: NO SOLUTION`: physically, a transaction where you only receive money and never pay anything out cannot balance to zero at any real interest rate! Likewise, always make sure your time period $N$ and periodic rate $I\%YR$ share the same time unit: for a 30-year monthly mortgage ($N = 360\text{ months}$), divide the annual nominal rate ($6.75\%$) by $12$ (`6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR]` $\to 0.5625\%/\text{month}$) before storing it—otherwise `6.75 [I%YR]` would model a loan charging $6.75\%$ interest *every single month* ($81\%\text{ APR}$)!

### 11.6.3 Financial Verification: Dedicated `[↰] [TVM]` Registers vs. Direct Stack Closed Forms
While the dedicated 5-variable `[↰] [TVM]` softkeys automate iterative and multi-register calculations, seasoned financial analysts often cross-check valuations by pairing the **5-Variable `[↰] [TVM]` Register Solver** with **Direct Inside-Out Closed-Form Evaluation on the 4-Level Stack**:

| Financial Instrument | Analytical Closed-Form Formula | Native RPN Inside-Out Recipe |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ordinary Annuity PV** | $PV = PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right]$ | `1 ENTER i + N +/- yˣ 1 x⇄y - i ÷ PMT ×` |
| **Ordinary Annuity FV** | $FV = PMT \left[ \frac{(1 + i)^N - 1}{i} \right]$ | `1 ENTER i + N yˣ 1 - i ÷ PMT ×` |
| **Amortization Payment** | $PMT = PV \left[ \frac{i}{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}} \right]$ | `1 ENTER i + N +/- yˣ 1 x⇄y - i x⇄y ÷ PV ×` |
| **Sinking Fund Payment** | $PMT = FV \left[ \frac{i}{(1 + i)^N - 1} \right]$ | `1 ENTER i + N yˣ 1 - i x⇄y ÷ FV ×` |
| **Perpetuity PV** | $PV = \frac{PMT}{i}$ | `PMT ENTER i ÷` |
| **Growing Perpetuity PV** | $PV = \frac{PMT}{i - g}$ | `PMT ENTER i ENTER g - ÷` |

For the master quick-reference tables of all financial mathematics, amortization, and TVM equations, consult **[Appendix D: Section 9 (Financial Mathematics, Amortization & TVM Equations)](sc32/appendix-d-constants-and-equations.md)**.

## 11.7 Capital Allocation, Bond Pricing, and Cash-Flow Modeling on the Stack

The following explorations progress from commercial invoice percentages and SaaS growth elasticity through residential and commercial mortgage amortization, bond duration, discounted cash-flow (DCF) valuation, and quantitative trading risk metrics.

### 11.7.1 Commercial Percentages, Margin Markup & Cash-Flow Foundations

We start with William Kahan's non-destructive `%` and `%CHG` operators and geometric compounding before moving into the 5-variable TVM solver.

Because `[↱] [%]` on an RPN stack replaces Register $X$ with $(Y \times X)/100$ while leaving the base contract amount untouched in Register $Y$, keying `85000 [ENTER] 17.5 [↱] [%]` in `[FIX] 2` mode displays the negotiated dollar concession ($X = \mathbf{\$14,875.00}$) alongside the $\$85,000.00$ list price in $Y$, and pressing `[-]` immediately yields the net invoice payable (**`$70,125.00`**, $X = \mathbf{70125.00}$).

#### Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR)
A venture capital fund invests $\$14.0\text{M}$ into an industrial robotics startup at Series A, and the company exits via acquisition for $\$88.5\text{M}$ exactly $n = 5\text{ years}$ later. Total multiple on invested capital is $88.5 / 14.0 = 6.32\times$, but what steady annual compounding rate—the **Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR)**—produces a $6.32\times$ expansion over five years? Taking the fifth root (`5 [1/x] [yˣ]`) of the terminal wealth ratio and subtracting $1$ gives the exact geometric mean annual return:

$$\text{CAGR} = \left(\frac{88.5}{14.0}\right)^{1/5} - 1$$

Keying `88.5 [ENTER] 14.0 [÷] 5 [1/x] [yˣ] 1 [-] 100 [×]` evaluates the terminal multiple, raises it to the $1/5$ power, subtracts $1$, and scales by $100$ to reveal a compound annual growth rate of **`44.60%`**:

| 01 | `88.5 [ENTER]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 88.50 | 88.50 | `88.50_` |
| 02 | `14.0 [÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 6.32 | `6.32` |
| 03 | `5 [1/x]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 6.32 | 0.20 | `0.20` |

| 06 | `100 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 44.60 | `44.60` |

#### First-Month Amortization Split & The Crossover Point
Why does your loan balance barely budge during the early years of a 30-year mortgage? Because each month, the bank first charges rent on the entire remaining debt ($I_1 = PV \times i$) and only applies whatever is left over of your monthly check ($P_1 = |PMT| - I_1$) toward reducing principal. On our $\$350,000$ mortgage at $0.5625\%/\text{month}$ ($PMT = -\$2,270.09$):
* Interest Month 1: $350,000 \times 0.005625 = \mathbf{\$1,968.75}$ ($86.7\%$ of payment)
* Principal Month 1: $\$2,270.09 - \$1,968.75 = \mathbf{\$301.34}$ ($13.3\%$ of payment)
* New Principal Balance: $\$350,000 - \$301.34 = \mathbf{\$349,698.66}$.

In fact, as the table below shows, the monthly principal reduction $P_k$ does not overtake the monthly interest charge $I_k$ until **Month 237**—nearly twenty years into the loan!

| Month | Remaining Balance | Monthly Payment | Interest ($I_k$) | Principal ($P_k$) | Equity % | Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **1** | $\$349,698.66$ | $\$2,270.09$ | $\$1,968.75$ | $\$301.34$ | $0.09\%$ | $86.7\%$ of payment goes to interest |
| **237** | $\$199,642.18$ | $\$2,270.09$ | $\$1,130.71$ | $\$1,139.38$ | $42.96\%$ | **Amortization Crossover:** $P_k > I_k$ |
| **360** | $\$0.00$ | $\$2,270.09$ | $\$12.70$ | $\$2,257.39$ | $100.00\%$ | Final payoff; $\$467,233.60$ total interest |

### 11.7.2 Fixed-Income Bonds, Mortgages & Lease Amortization

Storing four TVM variables and solving for the fifth (`N`, `I%YR`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV`) under strict cash-flow sign conventions also prices corporate bonds and multi-year acquisition targets.

#### Corporate Bond Yield to Maturity (YTM)
Suppose an investor buys a 10-year corporate bond ($N = 20$ semi-annual periods) with a $\$1,000.00$ par value ($FV = +\$1,000.00$) and a $5.5\%$ annual coupon paid semi-annually ($PMT = +\$27.50$ every six months) at a discounted market price of $\$925.00$ ($PV = -\$925.00$ cash outflow today). What is the bond's annualized **Yield to Maturity (YTM)**? Storing $N, PV, PMT,$ and $FV$ and pressing `[I%YR]` invokes the 240-interval bisection solver to find the semi-annual yield $i = 3.2666\%$, which we double (`2 [×]`) to obtain the bond-equivalent annual yield $\text{YTM} = \mathbf{6.53\%}$:

### 11.7.3 Everyday Carry Math & Compound Markdowns

Even outside the boardroom, keeping intermediate subtotals live on the four-level stack turns multi-way dinner splits and stacked retail markdowns into effortless one-pass calculations.

#### Banquet Check Split with Itemized Wine Separation
Eight colleagues dine out together and receive a grand total bill of $\$480.00$. Three of the eight guests shared two reserve bottles of wine totaling $\$96.00$, while everyone shared the food equally. How much should the wine drinkers and non-drinkers each pay? Deducting the wine tab via `480 [ENTER] 96 [-]` isolates the shared food bill $(\$384.00)$, and `8 [÷]` establishes the per-guest food share $(\$48.00)$ in Register $X$. Computing the per-drinker wine allocation via `96 [ENTER] 3 [÷]` places $\$32.00$ in $X$ while the $\$48.00$ food share waits in $Y$, so `[+]` resolves the wine-drinker total ($X = \mathbf{\$80.00}$) alongside **`$48.00`** for non-wine guests.

#### Retail Store Double Discount
A retail store advertises a "$30\%$ seasonal sale plus an extra $15\%$ VIP coupon" on a $\$280.00$ designer jacket. A casual shopper might add $30\% + 15\% = 45\%$ off, expecting to pay $\$154.00$—but successive percentage markdowns compound multiplicatively against the reduced subtotal rather than additively! Keying `280 [ENTER] 30 [↱] [%]` followed by `[-]` deducts the initial $30\%$ markdown $(\$84.00)$ to leave the sale price $(\$196.00)$ in Register $X$, and chaining `15 [↱] [%] [-]` applies the $15\%$ VIP coupon $(\$29.40)$ against that reduced base to yield $\mathbf{\$166.60}$—an effective combined discount of $1 - (0.70)(0.85) = 40.5\%$.

### 11.7.4 Real vs. Nominal Returns, Uneven IRR & Bond Duration

We next evaluate cumulative inflation erosion, uneven cash-flow internal rates of return (IRR) via `[↱] [SOLVE]`, and fixed-income Macaulay and modified duration.

#### Cumulative Inflation and Purchasing Power
A creeping inflation rate of $3.2\%$ per year sounds gentle in any single twelve-month window, but over two decades its exponential compounding quietly erodes uninvested cash. What will $\$100,000$ of uninvested cash buy in today's constant dollars after 20 years of $3.2\%$ average annual inflation?

$$PV = \frac{100,000}{(1.032)^{20}}$$

Deflating nominal currency by the cumulative CPI price-level factor $(1 + \pi)^{20}$ via `100000 [ENTER] 1.032 [ENTER] 20 [yˣ] [÷]` ($1.87756$ in the denominator) reveals that $3.2\%$ annual inflation erodes $\$100,000$ to **`53260.60`** ($\mathbf{\$53260.60}$) in constant-dollar purchasing power—cutting purchasing power nearly in half and shrinking an $84.0\text{ mm}$ 1-Whole purchasing-power column in the **84 mm Fraction Towers** down to nearly the $42.0\text{ mm}$ ($\frac{1}{2}$) block.

#### Internal Rate of Return (IRR) on Uneven Cash Flows
When a project produces *equal* periodic payments, `[↰] [TVM]` solves its yield in one keystroke. What if the annual cash flows are *uneven*? Suppose an infrastructure venture requires an upfront capital outlay of $C_0 = -\$100,000.00$ and generates rising year-end inflows of $C_1 = \$30,000.00, C_2 = \$40,000.00,$ and $C_3 = \$50,000.00$. To find the project's **Internal Rate of Return ($\text{IRR}$)**—the discount rate $r$ where Net Present Value ($\text{NPV}$) equals zero—we write $\text{NPV}(r) = 0$ in Horner nested form using the gross discount factor $x = 1 + r$ and hand it to Brent's root finder `[↱] [SOLVE]`:

$$NPV(r) = -100000 + \frac{30000}{1+r} + \frac{40000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{50000}{(1+r)^3} = 0$$

Let discount factor $x = 1+r$. In `[↱] [EQN]` mode, enter the Horner-nested polynomial in $x$:
`50000 X [÷] 40000 [+] X [÷] 30000 [+] X [÷] 100000 [-]`
Using `[↱] [SOLVE] X` with initial guess $x = 1.10$, the solver converges to $x = 1.08889 \implies r = x - 1 = \mathbf{8.89\%}$:

| Step | Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Display |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 01 | `1.10 [STO] X` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.10 | `1.10` |
| 02 | `[↱] [SOLVE]X` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.10 | 1.08889 | `1.08889` |
| 03 | `1 [-]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.10 | 0.08889 | `0.08889` |
| 04 | `100 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.10 | 8.89 | `8.89` |

#### Macaulay and Modified Duration of an Investment-Grade Bond
Why does a 3-year coupon bond behave like a slightly shorter-than-3-year zero-coupon bond when interest rates move? Because you receive part of your cash back early in Years 1 and 2 via the coupon payments! In 1938, economist Frederick Macaulay defined **Macaulay Duration ($D$)** as the present-value-weighted average time until a bond's cash flows arrive, and dividing by $(1 + y)$ gives **Modified Duration ($D^*$)**, which measures the percentage change in bond price per $1\%$ change in yield. Let's compute both for a 3-year $8.0\%$ annual coupon bond trading at par ($\$1,000.00$) with yield $y = 8.0\%$:

$$\text{Macaulay Duration } D = \frac{1 \times 80/1.08 + 2 \times 80/1.08^2 + 3 \times 1080/1.08^3}{1000} = \mathbf{2.783\text{ years}}$$
$$\text{Modified Duration } D^* = \frac{D}{1 + y} = \frac{2.783}{1.08} = \mathbf{2.577\text{ years}}$$
Physically, if you dock three present-value **84 mm Fraction Towers** at $t = 1, 2, 3\text{ years}$ proportional to the discounted cash flows ($\$74.07$, $\$68.59$, and $\$857.34$), Macaulay Duration $D = 2.783\text{ years}$ is the exact center-of-mass pivot point where the timeline balances, and a $100\text{ bps}$ ($1.0\%$ on the `0.01` hundredths socket of the **Place Value Cubes** tray) rise in market interest rates causes approximately a $2.58\%$ decline in bond price.

| 01 | `80 [ENTER] 1.08 [÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 74.0741 | `74.07` |
| 02 | `80 [ENTER] 1.08 [ENTER] 2 [yˣ] [÷] 2 [×] [+]` | 74.07 | 74.07 | 74.07 | 211.2483 | `211.25` |
| 03 | `1080 [ENTER] 1.08 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [÷] 3 [×] [+]` | 211.25 | 211.25 | 211.25 | 2783.2648 | `2783.26` |

### 11.7.5 The Executive Boardroom, Realtor Open-House & Trading Desk Playbook

Whether you are a Chief Executive Officer auditing unit economics during a board meeting, a commercial or residential realtor structuring an offer at an open house, or a quantitative trader sizing a position under market volatility, you do not have time to open a laptop spreadsheet. These high-velocity RPN workflows turn the SC-32 into an instant tactical advantage in any negotiation.

#### The CEO's Gross Margin vs. Markup Trap
One of the most expensive mistakes in retail and hardware manufacturing is confusing **Markup** (profit divided by *cost*) with **Gross Margin** (profit divided by *selling price*). Suppose a hardware product has a landed bill-of-materials cost of $C = \$60.00$, and the board mandates a **$40.0\%$ Gross Margin** on retail sales.
* **The Amateur Markup Trap:** Adding $40\%$ on top of $\$60.00$ (`60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%] [+]` $\rightarrow$ **`\$84.00`**) yields $\$24.00$ of profit on an $\$84.00$ price tag—which is only $\$24.00 / \$84.00 = 28.57\%$ gross margin!
* **True Gross Margin Pricing:** If gross profit takes $40\%$ of the selling price, then the $\$60.00$ cost must represent the remaining $1 - 0.40 = 60\%$ of the selling price ($\text{Price} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{1 - \text{Margin}}$):
  `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER] 0.40 [-] [÷]` $\rightarrow$ **`\$100.00`**.

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 60.00 | 24.00 | 40% markup on \$60.00 cost: \$24.00 |
| 02 | `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 84.00 | Flawed markup price: \$84.00 (28.57% margin) |
| 03 | `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]` | 84.00 | 60.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | True margin pricing: stage cost \$60 in $Z$ and 1.00 in $Y$ |
| 04 | `.40 [-]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 60.00 | 0.60 | 1 - 0.40 = 0.60 margin complement; \$60.00 drops to $Y$ |
| 05 | `[÷]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 84.00 | 100.00 | True gross margin retail price: \$100.00 |

#### The Realtor's Open-House Extra-Principal Payoff Hack
At an open house, a prospective buyer is hesitant about the 30-year ($360\text{-month}$) commitment on the $\$350,000.00$ mortgage at $6.75\%$ APR ($PMT = -\$2,270.09/\text{mo}$ from the 30-year residential mortgage analysis above). Because 86.7% of early payments go to interest, any extra principal added each month attacks the loan balance directly! Let's show the buyer what happens if they add just **$\$250.00/\text{month}$** in extra principal ($PMT = -\$2,520.09/\text{mo}$) and solve for the new payoff term `[N]` via `6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR] 350000 [PV] 0 [FV] 2520.09 [+/-] [PMT] [N]`, which drops the repayment horizon to **`270.93` months** ($22.6\text{ years}$):

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%YR]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.56 | Monthly rate i = 0.5625% |
| 02 | `350000 [PV] 0 [FV]` | 0.00 | 0.56 | 350000.00 | 0.00 | Store PV = \$350,000.00, FV = \$0.00 |
| 03 | `2520.09 [+/-] [PMT]` | 0.56 | 350000.00 | 0.00 | -2520.09 | Augmented payment: -\$2,520.09/mo |
| 04 | `[N]` | 0.56 | 350000.00 | 0.00 | 270.93 | Accelerated repayment: 270.93 months |

Adding $\$250/\text{month}$ eliminates **$89\text{ monthly payments}$ ($7.4\text{ years}$)** and saves **$\$134,474.66$** in lifetime interest.

#### Quantitative Trading Desk — Sharpe Ratio & Kelly Criterion Sizing
On a quantitative trading desk, raw return means nothing without knowing how much volatility risk was taken to earn it, and a winning edge can still bankrupt a fund if positions are oversized. Two classic metrics govern portfolio risk: Nobel laureate William Sharpe's **Sharpe Ratio** (excess return over the risk-free rate per unit of volatility) and Bell Labs physicist John Kelly's **Kelly Criterion** (the exact fraction of capital $f^*$ that maximizes long-run logarithmic wealth growth):
1. **Ex-Post Sharpe Ratio:** A systematic portfolio returns $R_p = 18.5\%$ while the risk-free Treasury bill rate is $R_f = 4.5\%$, with annualized return volatility $\sigma_p = 11.2\%$:
   $$\text{Sharpe} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_p}$$
   Normalizing the excess return via `18.5 [ENTER] 4.5 [-] 11.2 [÷]` yields a Sharpe Ratio of **`1.25`**.
2. **Kelly Criterion Optimal Position Size ($f^*$):** A trade setup has historical win rate $p = 0.56$ (loss rate $q = 0.44$) and average win-to-loss payoff ratio $b = 1.50$:
   $$f^* = \frac{b p - q}{b} \times 100$$
   Evaluating the expected edge via `1.5 [ENTER] 0.56 [×] 0.44 [-] 1.5 [÷] 100 [×]` yields an optimal full-Kelly allocation of **`26.67%`** of risk capital (most desk traders allocate "Half-Kelly" $= 13.33\%$ to dampen drawdown variance).

Normalizing excess portfolio return `18.5 [ENTER] 4.5 [-]` ($14.00\%$) by annualized return standard deviation `11.2 [÷]` yields William Sharpe's reward-to-variability ratio ($X = \mathbf{1.25}$). To maximize expected logarithmic capital growth $E[\ln(1 + f R)]$, John Kelly's information-theoretic sizing formula `1.5 [ENTER] 0.56 [×]` ($bp = 0.84$) less `0.44 [-]` ($0.40$) divided by `1.5 [÷] 100 [×]` yields the full-Kelly allocation ($Y = 1.25,\; X = \mathbf{26.67}\%$).
*(**`LASTX` Single-Entry Kelly Identity:** Rewriting Kelly's formula as $f^* = p - \frac{1 - p}{b}$ eliminates re-entering both $b = 1.5$ and $q = 1 - p$: keying `1 [ENTER] 0.56 [-] [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] 1.5 [÷] [-] 100 [×]` computes $1 - 0.56 = 0.44$ in $X$ while saving $p = 0.56$ in `LASTX`, recalls $0.56$ and swaps it into $Y$, divides $0.44 / 1.5$, and subtracts from $0.56$ to produce $\mathbf{26.67\%}$ with `0.56` and `1.5` each typed only once.)*

# Chapter 12: Function & Scatter Plotting Engine

## 12.1 Seeing the Invisible: Why One 64-Point Curve Reveals What a Thousand Numbers Hide

In 1637, French philosopher and mathematician René Descartes published *La Géométrie* *([Descartes, 1637](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-descartes1637))*, resolving a schism that had divided mathematics since antiquity. Geometry belonged to continuous space—to lines, circles, and figures drawn with straightedge and compass. Algebra belonged to discrete symbolic manipulation—to polynomial balances and abstract quantities. Descartes demonstrated that these two worlds are isomorphic: every algebraic relation $y = f(x)$ defines a geometric locus in coordinate space, and every geometric curve can be interrogated through its coordinates.

Centuries later, an engineer wrestling with complex systems—an oscillating LC circuit, an aerodynamic shockwave boundary, or the decay envelope of an underdamped suspension—faces the inverse dilemma. A stack of discrete numbers on a handheld calculator, no matter how precise, cannot immediately reveal a high-frequency resonance peak, a hidden vertical asymptote, or a saddle point. To see the dynamics of a physical system, one must see its shape.

The StackCalc SC-32 bridges this gap through its dedicated 64-point vector graphics engine (`[↱] [PLOT]`). By transforming the transflective dot-matrix LCD into a miniature Cartesian laboratory, the instrument evaluates 64 discrete mathematical slices across any domain and renders an interpolated continuous curve in under 42 milliseconds. Paired with interactive crosshair reticle tracing, the engineer can walk along the mathematical terrain, reading exact coordinate pairs from the real-time status bar and committing discovered extrema or inflection points directly back into the RPN operational stack with a single keystroke.

![SC-32 64-Point Vector Function Plotter ([↱] [PLOT]): Cubic Polynomial x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 with Interactive Crosshair](../assets/manuals/screenshots/sc32_plot_polynomial.png)

## 12.2 The Transflective 64-Point Vector Rendering Engine

While the StackCalc SC-32 is engineered primarily as a rapid tactile numerical instrument, its $132 \times 65$ transflective monochrome dot-matrix display features a dedicated **64-Point Vector Graphics Engine (`[↱] [PLOT]`)**, accessed via Right Shift `[↱]` on the multi-action `[x∥y]` key (Row 7, Column 3).

### 12.2.1 Viewport Geometry & Pixel Mapping
The physical display is partitioned into two specialized zones:
* **Graphing Viewport ($128 \times 52\text{ pixels}$):** World coordinates $(x, y)$ are projected onto screen pixel coordinates $(u, v)$ via linear transformation:
  $$u = \left\lfloor \frac{x - X_{\min}}{X_{\max} - X_{\min}} \times 127 \right\rfloor$$
  $$v = 51 - \left\lfloor \frac{y - Y_{\min}}{Y_{\max} - Y_{\min}} \times 51 \right\rfloor$$
  where $u \in [0, 127]$ maps horizontally from left to right, and $v \in [0, 51]$ maps vertically from top to bottom.
* **Status Readout Line ($132 \times 13\text{ pixels}$):** The lower 13 vertical pixels ($v \in [52, 64]$) are reserved for coordinate text readouts, equation labels, active mode indicators, and crosshair reticle telemetry rendered in high-contrast monospaced font.

### 12.2.2 Vector Line Rasterization & Bresenham Algorithm
Connecting 64 discrete sample points into a continuous graphic curve requires integer line interpolation. The SC-32 graphics pipeline executes a hardware-accelerated **Bresenham Vector Line Algorithm** directly into the 1,072-byte display frame buffer.
Given two adjacent plotted coordinates $(u_0, v_0)$ and $(u_1, v_1)$:
$$\Delta u = |u_1 - u_0|, \quad \Delta v = |v_1 - v_0|$$
The error term $\epsilon = 2\Delta v - \Delta u$ steps across pixel increments without floating-point division, drawing smooth 1-pixel wide line segments that preserve high-frequency crests and steep asymptotes.

> **Reflective Daylight Liquid-Crystal Pixels & Bresenham Stepper Quantization:** Why does the SC-32 display remain razor-sharp in direct midday sunlight where smartphone OLED screens wash out? Each pixel cell in a **transflective** (*transmissive + reflective*) liquid-crystal panel sits above a microscopic semi-mirror: outdoors, ambient sunlight passes through the liquid crystal, bounces off the rear reflector, and returns to your eye with zero battery drain; indoors, a warm edge-lit LED waveguide shines upward through the same liquid-crystal shutter. And when Jack Bresenham invented his 1965 integer line-drawing algorithm at IBM to connect $(u_0, v_0) \to (u_1, v_1)$ on a drum plotter, he solved the exact same discrete quantization problem that governs both our **Counting Tiles** grid (*Figure 12.2*) and every modern CNC mill or 3D printer $X/Y$ stepper carriage: by accumulating the integer decision residual $\epsilon = 2\Delta v - \Delta u$, the hardware knows on every horizontal column step whether to fire a vertical step pulse ($v \leftarrow v \pm 1$), tracing a continuous diagonal line using pure integer addition and subtraction.

### 12.2.3 Automatic Domain Scaling, Senary-Binary Root Detection & Tangent Overlays
When a mathematical function is plotted via `[↱] [PLOT]` across the graphing viewport:
1. **Domain Bounds Selection:** Domain bounds $[X_{\min}, X_{\max}]$ are read directly from stack registers $(Y, X)$—defaulting automatically to $[-3.0, +3.0]$ whenever $Y = X$ (or configured via `XMIN` and `XMAX` registers on the hardware viewport).
2. **Discrete Grid Evaluation (From the Counting & Array Studio Socket Grid to 64-Column Vector Sampling):** Just as docking $19.0 \times 19.0\text{ mm}$ tiles from the **Counting & Array Studio** into the discrete Miniblock socket grid on the Snapfinity lid—or aligning polynomial factors along the orthogonal axes of the **Algebra Factoring Studio L-Frame Stage**—quantizes continuous coordinates into discrete physical grid cells, the SC-32's hardware viewport sweeps **64 discrete sample columns** across $[X_{\min}, X_{\max}]$:
   $$x_k = X_{\min} + k \left( \frac{X_{\max} - X_{\min}}{63} \right), \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, 63$$
   For sample column $k = 21$ across the default domain $[-3.0, +3.0]$, this affine grid mapping on the 4-register stack illustrates how each pixel column maps to its exact domain abscissa $x_{21} = -1.000000$:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `3 [ENTER] 3 [+/-] [-]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 6.000000 | Total domain span $X_{\max} - X_{\min} = 3.0 - (-3.0) = 6.0$ |
| 02 | `63 [÷]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.095238 | Quantized column step $\Delta x = 6.0 / 63 \approx 0.095238$ |
| 03 | `21 [×]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 2.000000 | Horizontal displacement $k \cdot \Delta x = 2.0$ at column $k = 21$ |
| 04 | `3 [+/-] [+]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | -1.000000 | Sampled domain coordinate $x_{21} = X_{\min} + 2.0 = -1.000000$ |

3. **Automatic Vertical Range Scaling:** The internal min/max scan determines $Y_{\min} = \min(f(x_k))$ and $Y_{\max} = \max(f(x_k))$, ignoring non-finite singularities (`NaN` / $\pm\infty$). If $Y_{\max} - Y_{\min} < 10^{-12}$ (a flat constant line), the vertical range automatically pads to $[y - 1, y + 1]$.
4. **Automatic Root Marker Detection (6-Segment Senary Search + 30-Step Binary Search):** While generating the curve, the plotter automatically scans for zero crossings ($f(x_{k-1}) \cdot f(x_k) \le 0$). For each sign change, it executes a **5-pass Senary Search** (partitioning the interval into 6 equal sub-segments per pass to isolate the sub-interval containing the sign reversal), followed by a **30-iteration Binary Search** (bisection) to pinpoint the exact root $(x_{\text{root}}, 0)$ and place an interactive root marker directly on the curve.
5. **Central-Difference Tangent & Shaded Quadrature Overlays:** When invoked alongside numerical differentiation or Romberg integration (`[↱] [∫]`), the plotter superimposes the exact tangent line $y = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0)$ computed via central difference ($h = 10^{-5}$) or shades the Riemann area columns between $f(x)$ and $y = 0$. When no active equation is selected and at least two statistical data pairs reside in the **50-point scatter ring buffer**, `[↱] [PLOT]` automatically renders a bivariate scatter plot with the least-squares linear regression line $y = mx + b$ superimposed across the data range.
6. **Sub-Frame Latency:** Total plot generation and Bresenham rasterization completes in under **$42\text{ milliseconds}$**.

### 12.3.1 From Visual Curve Inspection to Stack Coordinate Commitment
Plotting a function on the transflective LCD immediately exposes its qualitative behavior—root crossings, asymptotic singularities, local extrema, and Gibbs ringing overshoots—before any numerical solver is invoked. Look at *Figure 12.2*: when you dock $19.0 \times 19.0\text{ mm}$ tiles from the **Counting & Array Studio** into the $3 \times 8$ discrete socket grid on the Snapfinity lid, a continuous diagonal line must step from socket column to socket column by integer grid increments $(\Delta u, \Delta v)$. That physical socket-grid quantization is the exact tactile model of the SC-32's $128 \times 52$ pixel framebuffer and Jack Bresenham's (1965) integer line-drawing algorithm: the plotter evaluates $y = f(x_k)$ at 64 discrete horizontal columns, maps each $(x_k, y_k)$ sample to its nearest integer pixel socket $(u_k, v_k)$, and connects adjacent sockets with 1-pixel staircase steps. Stepping the interactive crosshair reticle along the rasterized curve with `[↰] [↓]` and `[↰] [↑]` displays each sampled $(x, y)$ coordinate pair in real time (just like reading the simultaneous $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ sight-windows of the **Unit Circle Trigonometry Volvelle**). Pressing `[ENTER]` commits that exact coordinate pair directly into the operational stack ($Y = x, X = y$) so you can launch `[↱] [SOLVE]` or `[↱] [∫]` without retyping a single digit.

![Discrete Grid Sampling and Pixel Quantization Array](../assets/manuals/counting_tiles_array_3x8.png)

## 12.4 Window Bounds & Viewport Configuration

You can set the horizontal plotting window $[X_{\min}, X_{\max}]$ in two ways: either push the domain limits directly onto the stack ($Y = X_{\min},\; X = X_{\max}$, which defaults to $[-3.0, +3.0]$ whenever $Y = X$) and press `[↱] [PLOT]`, or store persistent bounds into the named window registers (`XMIN`, `XMAX`, `YMIN`, `YMAX`, `XSCL`, `YSCL`):

| Parameter | Register / Stack | Default Value | Description |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Xmin | Register $Y$ / `XMIN` | `-3.0` (Stack) / `-10.0` (Reg) | Leftmost domain boundary |
| Xmax | Register $X$ / `XMAX` | `+3.0` (Stack) / `+10.0` (Reg) | Rightmost domain boundary |
| Ymin | `YMIN` | (Auto-scaled) | Lower range boundary |
| Ymax | `YMAX` | (Auto-scaled) | Upper range boundary |
| Xscl | `XSCL` | 1.00000000000 | Tick mark spacing along X-axis |
| Yscl | `YSCL` | 1.00000000000 | Tick mark spacing along Y-axis |

For example, to sweep an equation from $-10$ to $+10$ on the fly, simply key `10 [+/-] [ENTER] 10 [↱] [PLOT]` (or store `10 [+/-] [STO] "XMIN"` and `10 [STO] "XMAX"` before pressing `[↱] [PLOT]`).

## 12.5 Advanced Statistical Regression Curve Overlays

When performing bivariate data analysis in `[↱] [SUMS]` mode, the SC-32 can superimpose four distinct mathematical curve models directly over your empirical scatter points:

| Model | Formula | Transformation Protocol |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Linear | $y = m x + b$ | Native coordinates: $(x, y)$ |
| Logarithmic | $y = a \ln(x) + b$ | Semi-logarithmic: $(\ln x, y)$ |
| Exponential | $y = a e^{b x}$ | Semi-logarithmic: $(x, \ln y)$ |
| Power | $y = a x^b$ | Log-Log: $(\ln x, \ln y)$ |

### 12.5.1 Goodness-of-Fit & Coefficient of Determination ($R^2$)
The correlation coefficient $r$ provided by `[ŷ]` quantifies the linear association between the transformed coordinates, and squaring $r$ on the stack (`[↰] [x²]`) yields the **Coefficient of Determination ($R^2$)**:

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{\text{res}}}{SS_{\text{tot}}} = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}$$

For the pressure sensor calibration dataset analyzed below ($r = 0.999565$), pressing `[↰] [x²]` immediately gives $R^2 = 0.999130$, confirming that $99.91\%$ of the output voltage variance is explained by applied pressure while the scatter plot lets you inspect the individual residuals visually.

## 12.6 Visual Crosshair Bracketing (`PLOT`) & Analytical Refinement (`SOLVE` & `∫`)

Why pair a 64-column graphical plotter with a 12-digit numerical root solver and integrator? Because human visual intuition and high-precision numerical algorithms have complementary blind spots!

A blind numerical root search (`[↱] [SOLVE]`) or definite integral (`[↱] [∫]`) on an unfamiliar nonlinear function can easily miss a second root, get trapped near a local extremum, or integrate right across a hidden vertical asymptote. Conversely, a 64-column pixel plot (`[↱] [PLOT]`) reveals the global shape of a function in under $42\text{ ms}$, but its horizontal cursor step is quantized to $\Delta x = (X_{\max} - X_{\min})/63$. On the SC-32, you combine both strengths into a seamless two-stage pipeline:
1. **Visual Crosshair Reconnaissance (`[↱] [PLOT]`):** Plot the active `[↱] [EQN]` over $[X_{\min}, X_{\max}]$. The plotter's automatic **6-segment senary + 30-step binary root detector** places visual markers on every zero crossing, while stepping the crosshair reticle with `[↰] [↓]` and `[↰] [↑]` lets you inspect peaks, troughs, and inflection points on the bottom status line.
2. **Direct Stack Handoff to `[↱] [SOLVE]` & `[↱] [∫]` via `[ENTER]`:** When the crosshair rests near a root or interval bound of interest, pressing `[ENTER]` exits `[↱] [PLOT]` and pushes the active crosshair coordinates directly onto the operational stack: Register $Y$ receives the horizontal coordinate $x$, and Register $X$ receives the vertical evaluated coordinate $y$. From there, you can immediately invoke Brent's solver (`[↱] [SOLVE]`) or Adaptive Romberg Quadrature (`[↱] [∫]`) to refine that visual reading to full **12-digit analytical precision** without re-typing a single coordinate!

Keep three practical habits in mind when plotting functions: first, make sure the lower domain bound is strictly less than the upper bound ($X_{\min} < X_{\max}$, otherwise `Error 01: INVALID DATA` is reported when `XMIN` $\ge$ `XMAX`); second, check that your angular mode (`[RAD]` vs. `[DEG]`) matches your domain bounds when plotting trigonometric waveforms (plotting $\sin x$ over $[-3.14, +3.14]$ while accidentally in Degrees mode will trace only a tiny $6.28^\circ$ ramp near the origin!); and third, whenever an equation hits a pole or undefined domain point (such as $1/0$ or $\ln(-1)$) at one of the 64 sample columns, the Bresenham renderer automatically lifts its virtual pen across the singularity rather than drawing a false vertical line connecting $-\infty$ to $+\infty$.

## 12.7 Visual Reconnaissance and Analytical Refinement Across Engineering Curves

On a conventional algebraic graphing calculator, defining a multi-term Fourier series or transfer function requires typing a deeply nested string of infix parentheses into a small formula editor, where a single mismatched bracket halts the plot with a `SYNTAX ERROR`. On the StackCalc SC-32, equations are evaluated directly on the four hardware stack registers ($X, Y, Z, T$) in under 42 milliseconds *([HP, 1991](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp32sii1991))*, and pressing `[ENTER]` while tracing hands the live $(x, y)$ crosshair coordinates straight back to the stack for 12-digit verification, root-finding (`[↱] [SOLVE]`), or integration (`[↱] [∫]`) *([Brent, 1973](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-brent1973); [Romberg, 1955](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-romberg1955))*.

### 12.7.1 Harmonic Waveforms, Damped Transients & Cartesian Function Plotting

We open by rendering Joseph Fourier's harmonic square-wave synthesis, an underdamped automotive shock-absorber transient, and a Fraunhofer single-slit optical diffraction pattern on the $128 \times 52$ pixel canvas.

#### Square Wave Synthesis via Fourier Harmonics
When Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier claimed in 1807 that *any* periodic waveform—even a flat-topped square wave with vertical jumps—could be constructed by adding together smooth sinusoidal waves, his contemporaries Lagrange and Laplace were incredulous. Yet as we stack odd harmonics of decreasing amplitude ($\sin t + \frac{1}{3}\sin 3t + \frac{1}{5}\sin 5t + \dots$), the fundamental $\sin t$ provides the main humps, the third harmonic $\frac{1}{3}\sin(3t)$ carves out the center peak to flatten the plateau, and the fifth harmonic $\frac{1}{5}\sin(5t)$ sharpens the corners while leaving a characteristic ripple across the top. Let's synthesize and plot the three-harmonic square wave across $t \in [-180.0^\circ, +180.0^\circ]$ in Degrees mode (`[DEG]`):

$$y(t) = \sin(t) + \frac{1}{3}\sin(3t) + \frac{1}{5}\sin(5t)$$

In `[↱] [EQN]` mode, store the postfix expression `T [SIN] T 3 [×] [SIN] 3 [÷] [+] T 5 [×] [SIN] 5 [÷] [+]` under label `FOURIER`, set the domain bounds via `180 [+/-] [STO] "XMIN"` and `180 [STO] "XMAX"`, and press `[↱] [PLOT]`:

| Plot Telemetry | Crosshair Readout | Curve Feature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Active Function** | `SIN(X) + SIN(3*X)/3` | Fundamental + odd harmonic square-wave synthesis |
| **Crosshair Cursor** | `X = 90.000000000`, `Y = 0.8666666667` | Central saddle trough between twin local maxima |

Stepping the crosshair with `[↰] [↓]` and `[↰] [↑]` to the center of the positive plateau at $t = 90.0^\circ$ reveals a slight central dimple flanked by two higher Gibbs-overshoot shoulders:
$$y(90^\circ) = \sin(90^\circ) + \frac{1}{3}\sin(270^\circ) + \frac{1}{5}\sin(450^\circ) = 1.0 - 0.333333 + 0.200000 = \mathbf{0.866667}$$
The status bar reads `X: 90.000000000    Y: 0.8666666667`. We can verify that exact harmonic sum at $t = 90^\circ$ on the RPN stack via 1 [ENTER] 3 [1/x] [-] 5 [1/x] [+] $\implies \mathbf{0.866667}$:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `90 [SIN]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.000000 | Fundamental harmonic $\sin(90^\circ) = 1.000000$ |
| 02 | `90 [ENTER] 3 [×] [SIN]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.000000 | -1.000000 | Third harmonic phase $\sin(270^\circ) = -1.000000$; fundamental lifts to Y |
| 03 | `3 [÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.000000 | -0.333333 | Scale third harmonic amplitude $-\frac{1}{3} = -0.333333$ |
| 04 | `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.666667 | Partial sum of 1st + 3rd harmonics ($0.666667$) |
| 05 | `90 [ENTER] 5 [×] [SIN]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.666667 | 1.000000 | Fifth harmonic phase $\sin(450^\circ) = 1.000000$; partial sum lifts to Y |
| 06 | `5 [÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.666667 | 0.200000 | Scale fifth harmonic amplitude $+\frac{1}{5} = 0.200000$ |
| 07 | `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.866667 | Three-harmonic square wave trough ordinate $y(90^\circ) = 0.866667$ |

#### Damped Harmonic Oscillator Transient Ringing
When a car tire strikes a speed bump and drops back onto level pavement at $t = 0$, the suspension coil spring tries to bounce the chassis up and down at its damped natural frequency $\omega_d$, while the hydraulic shock absorber dissipates kinetic energy into heat, wrapping the oscillation inside an exponential decay envelope $e^{-\zeta \omega_n t}$:

$$x(t) = e^{-\zeta \omega_n t} \cos(\omega_d t)$$
For an underdamped sports suspension with damping ratio $\zeta = 0.15$, natural frequency $\omega_n = 4.0\text{ rad/s}$ ($\zeta \omega_n = 0.60\text{ s}^{-1}$), and damped frequency $\omega_d = \omega_n\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2} = 3.9546\text{ rad/s}$:
$$x(t) = e^{-0.60 t} \cos(3.9546 t)$$

In Radians mode (`[RAD]`), enter `T 0.60 [×] [+/-] [eˣ] T 3.9546 [×] [COS] [×]` in `[↱] [EQN]`, set the domain via `0 [STO] "XMIN"` and `6 [STO] "XMAX"`, and press `[↱] [PLOT]`:

| Plot Telemetry | Crosshair Readout | Curve Feature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Active Function** | `EXP(-0.6*T)*COS(3.9546*T)` | Underdamped second-order exponential ringdown envelope |
| **Crosshair Cursor** | `X = 0.000000000`, `Y = 1.0000000000` | Initial peak displacement at $t = 0$ |

One second after hitting the bump ($t = 1.0\text{ s}$ in `RAD`), the shock absorber has bled the amplitude envelope down to $e^{-0.60} \approx 54.9\%$ while the phase $\omega_d t = 3.9546\text{ rad}$ ($226.6^\circ$) places the suspension near the bottom of its first rebound trough ([RAD] 0.6 [+/-] [eˣ] 3.9546 [COS] [×] $\implies \mathbf{-0.377160}$):

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `1 [ENTER] .60 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.600000 | Damping exponent $\zeta \omega_n t = 0.600000$ at $t = 1.0\text{ s}$ |
| 02 | `[+/-] [eˣ]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.548812 | Exponential decay envelope $e^{-0.60} = 0.548812$ |
| 03 | `1 [ENTER]` | 0.00 | 0.548812 | 1.000000 | 1.000000 | Stage time $t = 1.0\text{ s}$ for oscillatory phase; envelope lifts to Z |
| 04 | `3.9546 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.548812 | 3.954600 | Damped phase angle $\omega_d t = 3.954600\text{ rad}$; envelope drops to Y |
| 05 | `[COS]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.548812 | -0.687229 | Cosine carrier $\cos(3.9546\text{ rad}) = -0.687229$ |
| 06 | `[×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | -0.377160 | Instantaneous suspension displacement $x(1.0) = -0.377160\text{ m}$ |

#### Sinc Function Diffraction Pattern
Shine a coherent laser beam through a narrow rectangular slit onto a dark wall, or transmit a rectangular digital voltage pulse across a band-limited radio channel, and the resulting wave amplitude profile is governed by the same universal curve—the **sinc function**, which is the Fourier transform of a rectangular window:

$$y(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$$
Plotting $y(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$ over $x \in [-4\pi, +4\pi]$ (`-12.57 [STO] "XMIN"`, `12.57 [STO] "XMAX"`) in Radians mode (`[RAD]`) reveals the tall central diffraction bright fringe at $x = 0$ ($\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1.00$) flanked by alternating positive and negative side lobes that cross zero at every non-zero integer multiple of $\pi$ ($\pm\pi, \pm 2\pi, \pm 3\pi, \pm 4\pi$). At the half-lobe point $x = \pi/2$, keying [RAD] [↱] [π] 2 [÷] [SIN] [↰] [LASTX] [÷] yields $\mathbf{0.636620}$.

Notice how `[↰] [LASTX]` streamlines evaluating $\operatorname{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$ at any angle: forming the half-lobe argument `[RAD] [↱] [π] 2 [÷]` ($\pi/2 \approx 1.570796\text{ rad}$) and pressing `[SIN]` evaluates $\sin(\pi/2) = 1.000000$ in Register $X$ while automatically archiving the radian argument $\pi/2$ in `LASTX`. Chaining `[↰] [LASTX] [÷]` recalls $\pi/2$ into $X$, lifts $1.000000$ into $Y$, and divides to yield the exact half-lobe amplitude $2/\pi$ ($X = \mathbf{0.636620}$, or $-3.92\text{ dB}$) without re-computing $\pi/2$.

### 12.7.2 Singularities, Bifurcations & Bivariate Scatter Overlays

Next we inspect how the plotter handles rational poles, biochemical saturation plateaus, empirical `[Σ+]` calibration scatter plots, and quadrature phase circles.

#### Rational Function with Pole & Vertical Asymptote
In optics and control theory, rational functions of the form $f(x) = \frac{1}{x - x_0}$ appear whenever a physical denominator passes through zero—such as thin-lens magnification $M = \frac{f}{f - d_o}$ as an object crosses the focal point $d_o = f$. Let's examine $f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}$ over $x \in [0, 4]$:

Because $f(x)$ diverges to $-\infty$ as $x \to 2^-$ and plunges from $+\infty$ as $x \to 2^+$, naive plotting software often connects the two branches with a vertical line straight through $x = 2.0$. The SC-32's singularity guard detects the pole and renders the lower-left and upper-right hyperbolic branches cleanly separated. Sampling the upper branch at $x = 2.5$ (`2.5 [ENTER] 2 [-]` $\rightarrow 0.500000$, followed by `[1/x]`) confirms the ordinate ($X = \mathbf{2.000000}$).

#### Michaelis-Menten Hyperbolic Enzyme Kinetics
In Chapter 9, we linearized enzyme kinetics by taking reciprocals $(1/[S], 1/v)$ for a Lineweaver-Burk regression. With `[↱] [PLOT]`, we can inspect Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten's untransformed hyperbolic saturation curve directly over $[S] \in [0, 100\text{ mM}]$ for an enzyme with maximum turnover velocity $V_{\max} = 100.0\text{ }\mu\text{mol/min}$ and Michaelis constant $K_m = 15.0\text{ mM}$:

$$v = \frac{V_{\max} [S]}{K_m + [S]}$$
The plotted curve rises steeply near the origin ($v \approx \frac{V_{\max}}{K_m}[S]$ when active sites are mostly empty) and bends smoothly toward the horizontal asymptote $V_{\max} = 100$ as substrate floods the enzyme. Stepping the crosshair to $[S] = K_m = 15.0\text{ mM}$ visually confirms that $K_m$ is the exact substrate concentration where reaction velocity reaches half-maximum ($v = V_{\max}/2 = 50.0\text{ }\mu\text{mol/min}$). On the stack, evaluating the numerator `100 [ENTER] 15 [×]` forms $V_{\max}[S] = 1500.00$ in Register $X$ while saving $[S] = 15.0$ in `LASTX`; chaining `[↰] [LASTX] 2 [×] [÷]` forms the denominator $15 + 15 = 30.00$ and divides to yield $X = \mathbf{50.000000}$ with `15` typed only once.

#### Bivariate Statistical Scatter Plot: Sensor Calibration
Whenever you calibrate a laboratory sensor via `[Σ+]` (as in Chapter 9's thermistor and pressure calibration models), glancing at the correlation coefficient $r$ alone is never enough—you also want to *see* the data points against the fitted line to verify that no single point is an outlier or a nonlinear bend. Let's load four piezoresistive pressure sensor calibration pairs—$(10\text{ kPa}, 1.25\text{ V}), (20\text{ kPa}, 2.45\text{ V}), (30\text{ kPa}, 3.80\text{ V}), (40\text{ kPa}, 4.95\text{ V})$—by clearing statistics (`[↰] [CLEAR] [CLΣ]`), entering `1.25 [ENTER] 10 [Σ+]`, `2.45 [ENTER] 20 [Σ+]`, `3.80 [ENTER] 30 [Σ+]`, `4.95 [ENTER] 40 [Σ+]`, and pressing `[↱] [PLOT]` (`STAT`):

The LCD renders the four $2\times 2$ pixel dot markers—just like docking four **Counting Tiles** at discrete $(x_i, y_i)$ coordinates on the grid—and superimposes the least-squares linear regression trendline $y = 0.1245x + 0.0000$ directly through the cloud:

#### Lissajous Figure 1:1 Phase Trajectory
In 1857, French physicist Jules Antoine Lissajous bounced a narrow beam of light off mirrors attached to two tuning forks vibrating at right angles, projecting glowing geometric loops onto a lecture-hall screen. Today, electrical engineers perform the same test in oscilloscope $X\text{–}Y$ mode to compare the frequency and phase of two AC signals. When two equal-frequency sinusoids have an exact $90^\circ$ ($\pi/2\text{ rad}$) quadrature phase shift:

$$x(t) = \cos(t), \quad y(t) = \sin(t)$$
the parametric trajectory $(x(t), y(t))$ traces the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$—the exact electronic counterpart of rotating the **Unit Circle Volvelle** through phase angle $t$ while reading its orthogonal $\cos t$ and $\sin t$ sight-windows simultaneously. In `[RAD]` mode, evaluating `[↱] [π] 4 [÷] [ENTER]` ($t = \pi/4 \approx 0.785398$), pressing `[COS]` to form $x = \cos(\pi/4) \approx 0.707107$ in $X$ while $t$ waits in $Y$, and executing `[x⇄y] [SIN]` resolves $y = \sin(\pi/4)$ in $X$ alongside $x$ in $Y$ ($Y = 0.707107,\; X = \mathbf{0.707107}$)—or without `[ENTER]` via `[↱] [π] 4 [÷] [COS] [↰] [LASTX] [SIN]`.

### 12.7.3 Polar Radiation Patterns & Cubic Inflection Geometry

Exploring directional antenna radiation lobes and polynomial concavity transitions.

#### Four-Petal Quadrupole Polar Rose
When RF engineers arrange four antenna elements into a phased quadrupole array—or when an acoustic transducer vibrates in a quadrupole mode—constructive interference beams energy along the four $45^\circ$ diagonal bisectors ($\theta = 45^\circ, 135^\circ, 225^\circ, 315^\circ$), while destructive phase cancellation creates dead-silent nodal lines along the cardinal axes ($\theta = 0^\circ, 90^\circ, 180^\circ, 270^\circ$). Over $\theta \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ]$, the polar radiation gain follows the four-petal rose:

$$r(\theta) = 3 \sin(2\theta)$$

At the first-quadrant diagonal bisector $\theta = 45^\circ$, doubling the azimuth `45 [ENTER] 2 [×]` ($2\theta = 90.0^\circ$), taking `[SIN]` ($\sin 90^\circ = 1.000000$), and scaling by `3 [×]` (`45 [ENTER] 2 [×] [SIN] 3 [×]` $\implies \mathbf{3.0000}$) confirms the peak main-lobe gain ($X = \mathbf{3.000000}$) at the tip of the petal.

#### Third-Degree Polynomial Inflection & Concavity Transition
Imagine driving along a highway S-curve modeled by the cubic polynomial over $x \in [0, 4]$:

$$y(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 2$$

The first derivative $y'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x-1)(x-3)$ vanishes at the local hill crest $(1, 6)$ and the valley trough $(3, 2)$. Right in the middle, where the second derivative $y''(x) = 6x - 12 = 0$ vanishes at $x = 2$, lies the **inflection point** $(2, 4)$—the exact point along the S-curve where the road transitions from curving downward (concave-down, $y'' < 0$) to curving upward (concave-up, $y'' > 0$) and your steering wheel passes through dead center.

At the inflection abscissa $x = 2$, writing $y(x)$ in nested Horner form $y(x) = ((x - 6)x + 9)x + 2$ and pre-filling the 4-level stack via `2 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER] 6 [-] [×] 9 [+] [×] 2 [+]` evaluates the inflection ordinate ($X = \mathbf{4.000000}$) with `2` typed only once as Register $T$ replicates $x = 2.0$ down the stack on every multiplication:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `2 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER]` | 2.000000 | 2.000000 | 2.000000 | 2.000000 | Flood all four stack registers with inflection abscissa $x = 2.0$ |
| 02 | `6 [-]` | 2.000000 | 2.000000 | 2.000000 | -4.000000 | Innermost Horner factor $x - 6 = -4.0$; Register $T$ replicates $2.0$ |
| 03 | `[×] 9 [+]` | 2.000000 | 2.000000 | 2.000000 | 1.000000 | Second Horner stage $(x - 6)x + 9 = 1.0$; $x = 2.0$ drops into $Y$ |

### 12.7.4 Structural Deflection & Torsion Profiles

We conclude by contrasting the cubic-parabolic bending curve of a cantilevered beam against the linear torsional windup of a transmission drive shaft.

#### Euler-Bernoulli Cantilever Beam Deflection Profile
Picture a structural steel balcony I-beam—or an aircraft wing spar—clamped rigidly into a concrete wall at $x = 0$ and supporting a concentrated point load $P$ at its free tip $x = L = 4.0\text{ m}$. Because the wall prevents the root from either sinking ($y(0) = 0$) or tilting ($y'(0) = 0$), integrating the Euler-Bernoulli bending-moment equation $EI y''(x) = P(L - x)$ twice produces the classic cubic-parabolic elastic curve:

$$y(x) = \frac{P x^2}{6 E I} (3L - x)$$

Over $x \in [0, L]$, the beam emerges horizontally from the wall, curves downward with increasing slope as the $x^2$ factor grows, and reaches its maximum tip deflection $\delta_{\max} = \frac{P L^3}{3 E I}$ at $x = L$. Given a flexural rigidity factor $\frac{P}{6EI} = 3.0625 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^{-2}$ on a $L = 4.0\text{ m}$ span, evaluating the span factor at the tip (`4 [ENTER] 3 [×] 4 [-]` $\rightarrow 3L - x = 8.0\text{ m}$), multiplying by $x^2$ (`4 [↰] [x²] [×]` $\rightarrow 128.0\text{ m}^3$), and scaling by `3.0625 [E] 5 [+/-] [×]` yields the exact tip deflection ($X = \mathbf{0.003920}\text{ m} = 3.92\text{ mm}$).
*(**`LASTX` Single-Entry Tip Evaluation:** Keying `3 [ENTER] 4 [×] [↰] [LASTX] [-] [↰] [LASTX] [↰] [x²] [×] 3.0625 [E] 5 [+/-] [×]` uses `[↰] [LASTX]` twice in succession to recover $x = 4.0\text{ m}$—first after `4 [×]` and again after `[-]`—so `4` is typed only once.)*

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `3 [ENTER] 4 [×]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 12.000000 | Compute $3L = 12.0\text{ m}$; tip coordinate $x = 4.0\text{ m}$ archived in `LASTX` |
| 02 | `[↰] [LASTX] [-]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 8.000000 | Recall $x = 4.0\text{ m}$ and subtract for span factor $3L - x = 8.0\text{ m}$ |
| 03 | `[↰] [LASTX] [↰] [x²] [×]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 128.000000 | Recall $x = 4.0\text{ m}$ again, square to $16.0\text{ m}^2$, and form $x^2(3L - x) = 128.0\text{ m}^3$ |
| 04 | `3.0625 [E] 5 [+/-] [×]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.003920 | Scale by $\frac{P}{6EI} = 3.0625 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^{-2}$; tip deflection $\delta_{\max} = 0.003920\text{ m}$ |

#### Elastic Torsion Twist Profile Along a Drive Shaft
Unlike a cantilevered beam whose bending moment varies along its length, a uniform circular drive shaft of polar moment $J$ and shear modulus $G$ transmitting torque $T$ from an engine gearbox ($x = 0$) to a rear differential ($x = 2.50\text{ m}$) experiences the *exact same* internal torque $T$ at every cross-section. Under Saint-Venant pure torsion, the angular twist $\theta(x) = \frac{T x}{J G}$ therefore plots as a straight line through the origin with constant torsional gradient $d\theta/dx = T/(JG) = 0.0045\text{ rad/m}$. Staging the shaft length `2.5 [ENTER]` ($2.50\text{ m}$), multiplying by the specific twist rate (`0.0045 [×]` $\rightarrow 0.011250\text{ rad}$), and converting radians to degrees (`180 [×] [↱] [π] [÷]`) resolves the total angular windup at the output flange ($X = \mathbf{0.644578}^\circ$).

# Chapter 13: Applied STEM Engineering Case Studies

## 13.1 The Chief Engineer's Pocket Notebook: The Physical Reality of G-Forces, Thermal Expansion, and Tolerance Stacks

Long before laptop CAD suites and cloud finite-element solvers, practicing engineers relied on a pocket notebook paired with a dedicated handheld calculator. Whether standing beneath the roaring cryogenic test stand of the Saturn V at Rocketdyne, walking the catwalk of a high-temperature ethylene cracking plant, or sighting through a theodolite across an alpine triangulation ridge, the chief engineer understood a fundamental truth: physical reality does not wait for a simulation grid to mesh.

In the physical world, thermal expansion shears bolts that look adequate on paper. Non-Newtonian shear thinning clogs micro-extrusion nozzles in additive manufacturing. High-frequency RF phase angles destroy amplifier efficiency if line impedances mismatch by even a few milliohms. In these critical environments, the StackCalc SC-32 serves not merely as an arithmetic tool, but as a live tactile flight deck for dimensional verification and physical intuition.

Every investigation in this chapter is taken from authentic field engineering practice—from the fluid dynamics of melted thermoplastic beads when 3D-printing our **Planetary Geared Clock** and $42.0\text{ mm}$ Gridfinity studio bins, to Carnot heat engines, acoustic crossovers, thin-lens optics, Hohmann orbital transfers, geodetic azimuth closures with the **Unit Circle Volvelle**, and statistical root-sum-square (RSS) mechanical tolerance stackups. By structuring physical equations into lean, parenthesis-free RPN operational stacks, you preserve intermediate variables directly in physical registers, ensuring that numbers never lose their connection to physical dimensions, forces, and material limits.

## 13.2 Cross-Disciplinary Harmonic Isomorphisms

Across electrical, optical, mechanical, and thermal engineering, identical mathematical operators govern seemingly distinct physical phenomena.

### 13.2.1 Cross-Disciplinary Mathematical Isomorphisms via `[x∥y]`
The Gaussian thin-lens equation ($\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$), parallel electrical resistance ($R_1 \parallel R_2$), series mechanical spring compliance ($k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 \parallel k_2$), multi-layer thermal conduction resistance ($\theta_{\text{eq}} = \theta_1 \parallel \theta_2$), and **compound belt/pulley or planetary gear speed-torque harmonic ratios** all share the exact harmonic formulation $x \parallel y = \frac{xy}{x+y}$. By providing the dedicated hardware operator `[x∥y]`, the SC-32 enables students and engineers to execute these computations in three stack tokens without intermediate reciprocal transformations—and opens direct algebraic cross-checks across seemingly unrelated disciplines. For instance, in our Arrhenius activation energy analysis below (and Synthesis Challenge 2), the reciprocal temperature denominator $\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}$ of the Arrhenius activation energy law can be evaluated either via explicit reciprocals (`300 [1/x] 350 [1/x] [-] [÷]`) or via signed harmonic combination (`300 [ENTER] 350 [+/-] [x∥y] [×]`, since $\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)^{-1} = \frac{T_1(-T_2)}{T_1 - T_2} = T_1 \parallel (-T_2)$) with zero `[1/x]` keystrokes. Likewise, our mechanical tolerance analysis below evaluates 3D mechanical tolerance stackups both via squared-variance summation (`[↰] [x²] [+] [√x]`) and via two chained polar norm conversions (`[↰] [▸θ,r]`).

---

## 13.3 Physical Unit & Mode Discipline in Field Calculations

Before stepping into the field investigations, keep three physical guardrails in mind—each one responsible for famous real-world engineering mishaps when overlooked:
- **Angular Mode Discipline (`[DEG]` vs. `[RAD]`):** Civil land surveying and antenna azimuth bearings are measured in compass degrees (`[DEG]`), whereas orbital mechanics, rotational kinematics, and AC harmonic phasors require radians (`[RAD]`). Always glance at the `RAD` status annunciator before pressing `[SIN]`, `[COS]`, or `[↱] [▸y,x]`.
- **Absolute Thermodynamic Temperature (Kelvin vs. Celsius):** In Carnot heat engines and Arrhenius chemical reaction rates, temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy and **must** be entered in absolute **Kelvin** ($T_{\text{K}} = T_{^\circ\text{C}} + 273.15$). Plugging Celsius temperatures directly into $1 - T_C/T_H$ treats the freezing point of water ($0^\circ\text{C}$) as absolute zero and produces nonsensical efficiencies!
- **Optical Focal Singularities ($d_o = f$):** When an object sits right at the focal point of a converging lens ($d_o = f$), the emerging light rays are collimated parallel and the image forms at infinity ($d_i \to \infty$), so evaluating $d_i = \frac{f \cdot d_o}{d_o - f}$ properly flags `ERROR 0: DIVIDE BY ZERO`.

## 13.4 Multidisciplinary Field Investigations: From Additive Manufacturing to Room Acoustics

In multidisciplinary field engineering—whether evaluating Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation $\Delta v = v_e \ln(m_0/m_f)$, Carl Friedrich Gauss's thin-lens law $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$, or Leonhard Euler's column buckling formula $P_{\text{cr}} = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{L^2}$—an algebraic calculator forces the practitioner into an error-prone ritual of nested parentheses. On the StackCalc SC-32, physical quantities flow from the inside out across the 4-register operational stack ($X, Y, Z, T$) with zero parentheses *([HP, 1982](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982); [Horowitz & Hill, 2015](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-horowitz2015))*, keeping every intermediate physical dimension visible on the screen.

### 13.4.1 Fluid Mechanics & 3D Printing Extrusion Dynamics

Why do high-speed 3D printers suddenly start clicking, under-extruding, or delaminating when you push print speeds too high? Inside the heated brass nozzle block, solid $1.75\text{ mm}$ polymer filament is fed from the top and must absorb enough thermal energy by conduction to melt completely into a low-viscosity fluid before being squeezed through a $0.40\text{ mm}$ orifice. Every hotend heater block has a maximum **volumetric melt flow rate** $\dot{Q}_{\max}$ (measured in $\text{mm}^3\text{/s}$). Push polymer through faster than $\dot{Q}_{\max}$, and an unmelted solid core reaches the nozzle tip, jamming the extruder gear!

**Hotend Extrusion Bead Fluid Dynamics Model:**

| Extrusion Parameter | Symbol & Formula | Verified Value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Line Width** | $w$ | $0.45\text{ mm}$ |
| **Layer Height** | $h$ | $0.20\text{ mm}$ |
| **Cross-Sectional Bead Area** | $A = w \times h = 0.45 \times 0.20$ | $0.09\text{ mm}^2$ |
| **Printhead Linear Velocity** | $v$ | $180\text{ mm/s}$ |
| **Volumetric Flow Rate** | $\dot{Q} = A \times v = 0.09 \times 180$ | **$16.2\text{ mm}^3\text{/s}$** |

#### Volumetric Melt Flow Rate Threshold
Suppose your slicer profiles a $0.40\text{ mm}$ brass nozzle to lay down tracks of width $w = 0.45\text{ mm}$ and layer height $h = 0.20\text{ mm}$ while the CoreXY printhead travels at linear speed $v = 180.0\text{ mm/s}$. Your hotend is rated for a maximum volumetric melt rate of $\dot{Q}_{\max} = 16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$. Keying `.45 [ENTER] .20 [×] 180 [×]` computes the cross-sectional bead area $A = w \times h$ and multiplies by the toolhead velocity $v$ to give the exact volumetric flow demand **`16.2`** ($\mathbf{16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}}$):

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `.45 [ENTER]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.450000 | 0.450000 | Extruded bead line width $w = 0.45\text{ mm}$ staged in $Y$ |
| 02 | `.20 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.090000 | Cross-sectional bead area $A = w \times h = 0.090000\text{ mm}^2$ |
| 03 | `180 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 16.200000 | Volumetric extrusion rate $\dot{Q} = A \times v = 16.200000\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$ |

#### Maximum Permissible Print Speed Inversion
Now flip the design question around: if you know your hotend's volumetric ceiling is $\dot{Q}_{\max} = 16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$ and you are printing structural layers of width $w = 0.45\text{ mm}$ and height $h = 0.20\text{ mm}$, what is the fastest linear toolhead speed $v_{\max}$ you can program into the slicer without outrunning the heater block?
$$v_{\max} = \frac{\dot{Q}}{w \times h} = 16.2 \div 0.45 \div 0.20 = \mathbf{180.0\text{ mm/s}}$$

Notice how RPN sequential division via `16.2 [ENTER] .45 [÷] .20 [÷]` divides by both denominator factors in place to return **`180`** ($X = \mathbf{180.0000}\text{ mm/s}$) without needing parentheses around $(w \times h)$.

#### Filament Part Mass & Feeder Drive Linear Speed
Conservation of mass dictates that every cubic millimeter of melted plastic exiting the tiny $0.40\text{ mm}$ nozzle per second must be pushed into the top of the hotend as solid $1.75\text{ mm}$ filament ($r = 0.875\text{ mm}$). Suppose we are printing a technical instrument enclosure with solid volume $V = 125.0\text{ cm}^3$ ($125,000\text{ mm}^3$) out of PLA bioplastic ($\rho = 1.24\text{ g/cm}^3$). Let's find both the finished part mass (to make sure enough filament remains on the spool) and the linear speed $v_f$ at which the cold-end drive gear feeds the $1.75\text{ mm}$ filament wire at peak flow ($\dot{Q} = 16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$):
1. Total part mass: $m = 125 \times 1.24 = \mathbf{155.0\text{ grams}}$.
2. Standard $1.75\text{ mm}$ filament ($r = 0.875\text{ mm}$) cross-sectional area:
   $$A_f = \pi r^2 = \pi \times 0.875^2 \approx 2.405282\text{ mm}^2$$
3. Linear feed velocity $v_f$ of the extruder drive gear at maximum flow ($16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$):
   $$v_f = \frac{\dot{Q}}{A_f} = \frac{16.2}{\pi \times 0.875^2} \approx \mathbf{6.735177\text{ mm/s}}$$

Scaling enclosure volume by PLA density `125 [ENTER] 1.24 [×]` gives the net part mass ($X = \mathbf{155.0000}\text{ g}$), while staging `16.2 [ENTER] .875 [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×]` forms the feedstock cross-section $A_f = \pi r^2 \approx 2.4053\text{ mm}^2$ in Register $X$ beneath $\dot{Q} = 16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$ in Register $Y$ so `[÷]` resolves the filament inlet velocity ($X = \mathbf{6.7352}\text{ mm/s}$):

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `16.2 [ENTER]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 16.200000 | 16.200000 | Stage volumetric melt flow rate $\dot{Q} = 16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$ in $Y$ |
| 02 | `.875 [↰] [x²]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 16.200000 | 0.765625 | Square filament radius $r^2 = 0.875^2 = 0.765625\text{ mm}^2$ |
| 03 | `[↱] [π] [×]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 16.200000 | 2.405282 | Feedstock cross-sectional area $A_f = \pi r^2 = 2.405282\text{ mm}^2$ |
| 04 | `[÷]` | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 6.735177 | Cold-end extruder feed velocity $v_f = \dot{Q}/A_f = 6.735177\text{ mm/s}$ |

#### Extruder Stepper Motor Pulse Rate
With the cold-end filament feed speed $v_f \approx 6.735177\text{ mm/s}$ sitting right in Register $X$ from the filament feed calculation above, how many step pulses per second must the printer's microcontroller send to a planetary-geared extruder stepper motor calibrated at $415.0\text{ microsteps/mm}$?
$$f_{\text{step}} = v_f \times \text{steps/mm} = \frac{16.2}{\pi \times 0.875^2} \times 415.0 \approx \mathbf{2,795.10\text{ Hz}}$$

Simply multiplying the unrounded filament feed velocity in Register $X$ (`16.2 [ENTER] .875 [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] [÷]`) by `415.0 [×]` yields the exact stepper interrupt rate ($X = \mathbf{2795.0983}\text{ Hz}$). Notice how this four-stage extrusion sequence brings our entire hardware-and-curriculum arc full circle: the $\rho = 1.24\text{ g/cm}^3$ bioplastic PLA density and $h = 0.20\text{ mm}$ layer-height geometry are the exact engineering specifications used in the hero calculation on the opening page of this manual ([**Index**](sc32/index.md) and [**Chapter 1**](sc32/01-craftsmanship-hardware.md)). Keeping $\dot{Q} \le 16.2\text{ mm}^3/\text{s}$ and $f_{\text{step}} \le 2.80\text{ kHz}$ prevents over-extrusion swell on the involute gear teeth of our **Planetary Geared Clock** (*Figure 13.2*), preserving the $0.20\text{ mm}$ radial backlash clearance required for the $12:1$ compound planetary carrier to spin freely.

### 13.4.2 Thermodynamics & Heat Transfer

In power-plant engineering and chemical process design, two thermodynamic questions dominate every heat-recovery loop: what is the maximum fraction of thermal energy that the laws of physics allow us to convert into mechanical work, and how much heat crosses the steel tubes of a counterflow heat exchanger?

#### Carnot Heat Engine Efficiency Upper Bound
In 1824, a 27-year-old French military engineer named Sadi Carnot proved a startling theorem: even an ideal, frictionless heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at absolute temperature $T_H$ and a cold sink at $T_C$ can never convert $100\%$ of its heat input into mechanical work, because a minimum fraction $T_C / T_H$ must be rejected to the cold sink to carry away entropy. Suppose a geothermal binary power plant runs its vapor turbine from a brine source at $T_H = 185^\circ\text{C}$ and condenses the working fluid with cooling water at $T_C = 22^\circ\text{C}$. Converting both temperatures to Kelvin ($+273.15$):
$$T_H = 185 + 273.15 = 458.15\text{ K}, \quad T_C = 22 + 273.15 = 295.15\text{ K}$$
$$\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{295.15}{458.15} = 0.355778 \quad (\mathbf{35.58\%})$$

Converting both reservoirs to Kelvin on the stack and subtracting their ratio from unity via `22 [ENTER] 273.15 [+] 185 [ENTER] 273.15 [+] [÷] 1 [x⇄y] [-]` yields the Carnot upper-bound efficiency **`0.355778`**:

| Step | Keystrokes | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 01 | `22 [ENTER] 273.15 [+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 295.150000 | Cold sink absolute temperature $T_C = 295.15\text{ K}$ |
| 02 | `185 [ENTER] 273.15 [+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 295.150000 | 458.150000 | Hot reservoir absolute temperature $T_H = 458.15\text{ K}$; $T_C$ lifts to $Y$ |
| 03 | `[÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.644221 | Absolute temperature ratio $T_C / T_H = 0.644221$ |
| 04 | `1 [x⇄y] [-]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.355778 | Carnot upper-bound efficiency $\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - T_C/T_H = 35.58\%$ |

#### Counterflow Heat Exchanger Log-Mean Temperature Difference (LMTD)
Why do industrial shell-and-tube heat exchangers pump hot turbine lube oil and cold cooling water in *opposite* directions (counterflow)? Because counterflow maintains a strong thermal driving difference along the entire tube length and can cool the exiting oil below the exiting water's temperature! Since the local temperature gap $\Delta T(x)$ decays exponentially along the tubes, integrating $dQ = U\,\Delta T(x)\,dA$ shows that the true effective driving difference is not the simple average $(\Delta T_1 + \Delta T_2)/2$, but the **Logarithmic Mean Temperature Difference (LMTD)**. Suppose hot oil cools from $T_{h1} = 120^\circ\text{C}$ to $T_{h2} = 65^\circ\text{C}$ against cooling water rising from $T_{c1} = 20^\circ\text{C}$ to $T_{c2} = 45^\circ\text{C}$:
$$\Delta T_1 = T_{h1} - T_{c2} = 120 - 45 = 75^\circ\text{C}, \qquad \Delta T_2 = T_{h2} - T_{c1} = 65 - 20 = 45^\circ\text{C}$$
$$\text{LMTD} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)} = \frac{75 - 45}{\ln(75 / 45)} = \frac{30}{\ln(1.666667)} \approx \mathbf{58.73^\circ\text{C}}$$

Evaluating the terminal difference `75 [ENTER] 45 [-]` ($30.0^\circ\text{C}$), forming the log-ratio `75 [ENTER] 45 [÷] [LN]` ($0.5108$ in $X$ while $30.0$ waits in $Y$), and dividing via `[÷]` establishes the effective thermal driving potential ($X = \mathbf{58.7285}^\circ\text{C}$—noticeably lower than the naive arithmetic average of $60.0^\circ\text{C}$!).
*(**`LASTX` Single-Entry LMTD Evaluation:** To evaluate $\frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)}$ without typing `75` and `45` twice, duplicate $\Delta T_1 = 75$ upfront and recover $\Delta T_2 = 45$ from `LASTX`: keying `75 [ENTER] [ENTER] 45 [-] [x⇄y] [↰] [LASTX] [÷] [LN] [÷]` computes $\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2 = 30.0$ while preserving `45` in `LASTX`, swaps `75` back to $X$, divides by `[↰] [LASTX]` ($45$), takes `[LN]`, and divides into `30.0` to produce $\mathbf{58.7285^\circ\text{C}}$ with each terminal temperature difference entered only once.)*
